The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative is a collaborative that is making significant strides in thoroughly vetting and meticulously documenting image biomarkers, thereby fostering their widespread adoption across various applications and domains. To achieve this goal, IBSI has established a knowledge base where all its standards, guidelines, and best practices are centrally located and systematically organised. Furthermore, IBSI utilizes a semantic framework that ensures its knowledge is easily interconnected with other relevant pieces of information. A case study demonstrates how IBSI utilizes the standard to link image biomarkers with other vital information and show their implications in domain-specific contexts. By openly providing access to its knowledge base, IBSI facilitates seamless feedback and input from the broader community, thereby fueling a future ecosystem of applications and services that will enable the seamless sharing and interchanging of data and knowledge.

We have analyzed the effects of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on kaon photoproduction. Two covariant isobar models were employed to simulate this process, with the formalism for high-spin propagators and interaction Lagrangians adopted from existing works. Different models yielded similar trends in form factors as long-range kaon regge trajectories were projected. Incorpororing high-spin resonances significantly improved the models' agreement with experimental data on observables and structure functions. Notably, including high-spin resonances improved the models' resonance structure and significantly reduced discrepancies between models and data. This suggested that high-spin resonances must contribute to kaon photoproduction.

This research describes the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset comprising 55,134 images. The methodology section delves into the individual steps of the pre-processing sequence, with section two offering a comprehensive overview of these stages. Section three provides detailed descriptions and calculations using OpenCV functionalities to illustrate each step in the pipeline, ultimately concluding with a retrospective evaluation of potential enhancements.

Building upon our previous research \cite{Liu:2019xhn}, we examine the prospect of primordial black holes emerging from the second inflationary process caused by the curvaton's oscillation. We employ the instability of the Mathieu equation to leverage the $\delta$ function, which enables a comprehensive representation of the power spectrum. Given the varying curvaton mass, we simulate a broad range of primordial black hole masses, highlighting three distinct scenarios. Initially, an oscillation driven by the curvaton results in primordial black holes accounting for all dark matter. In the second scenario, an additional contribution from the kinetic power spectrum increases the primordial black hole mass distribution, aligning with certain dark matter observations. As a final possibility, we show that late-time oscillations from the instability can generate primordial black holes with masses aligning with the observed dark matter density, assuming the late-time oscillation accounts for the reheating temperature and dark matter density.

University administrators and educational researchers are concerned with understanding enrollment patterns at a large scale but often rely on decisions made without a solid analytical foundation for student course enrollment behavior. A probabilistic framework can provide a clearer picture, drawing from multilabel classification and mixture models. By using historical data from a large university, a latent variable model based on the Gaussian distribution was built to learn course enrollment probabilities, offering a diverse set of analysis capabilities and robustness against incomplete data. The model performed favorably compared to other approaches such as deep learning methods, effectively revealing underlying factors that drive student interest in specific courses, including course difficulty attributes.

Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is resolved through a differential game approach. This study explores various information network configurations, beginning with the 'range' topology where control input distance is the primary concern. A key finding involves deriving optimal control inputs and their costimilarity, yieldability, and frequency of use. Additionally, it was determined that the largest possible range-based control input is a singular control function. Furthermore, it was discovered that the optimal range-based control is not influence-free but can be approximated as such when the range becomes sufficiently small. Subsequently, the study examines the 'range-roadwork' topology, where the distance is complemented by a horizontal position input. A key discovery in this context involved determining that optimal control values do not have upper or lower limits. As a complementary analysis, the study examines a key property of the range-roadtopology, referred to as 'influence-freedom', and revealed that such optimal control values can be approximated as independent of previous states when the range becomes sufficiently small, turning out to be a basic requirement for optimal control values in this context.

One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively reducing loss function estimates. When executing SGD on distributed machines, the algorithm necessitates substantial data exchange between the machines and the optimizer. Previous research has quantified the communication requirements of SGD, while our study focuses on enhancing communication efficiency by adapting SGD to the scale-up model and integrating straggler mitigation techniques via the Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD) approach. This method reduces communication needs by distributing the gradient computation among the machines and the optimizer. We combine CA-SGD with techniques that accommodate failing machines, thereby reducing communication complexity to $\mathcal{O}(N^{3/4 + \alpha})$ for optimization objectives, where $\alpha$ represents the parameter indicating the optimization problem's smoothness and data non-monotonicity. We observe that our results hold for any given $\alpha$ and note that the optimal communication complexity occurs when $\alpha = 1$. For specific machine learning applications such as ResNet, Inception, and Net, our algorithm's communication efficiency is observed to be 13.64 times better than traditional SGD, thereby yielding substantial speedups with large system sizes.

The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media significantly impacts public perception and user behavior, with generative models now making it quicker and cheaper to produce fake content. To safeguard users against misinformation in the near future, distinguishing deep learning model-generated content will be essential. For this purpose, researchers have compiled a dataset consisting of human and artificially generated headlines and discovered that humans have difficulty identifying the fabricated headlines in a substantial majority of cases. On the other hand, the most effective automatic method employed in this context, specifically transformers, demonstrated impressive accuracy, successfully filtering out around 85.7% of the content produced by language models as being fabricated and accurately identifying 57.3% of the content as being written by humans.

In polycrystalline, amorphous, and ion-damaged Kitaev materials, we observe the spontaneous breaking of inversion symmetry, giving rise to a chiral spin liquid. The chiral spin liquid's robust nature is caused by a spontaneously developing time-re reversal symmetry that's associated with it. The magnitude of the NMR shift in this chiral state directly correlates with the angle between neighboring tetrahedra in the material, providing insight into the local structure. Using $^{125}$Te NMR, we've found that the angles between tetrahedra within partially amorphized Na$_2$Cu$_3$Te$_3$O$_2$ are significantly disordered when the material is irradiated, confirming the role of atomic displacement in generating chirality locally within the material structure.

Future large-scale radio interferometers, aiming to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances, may struggle with computing cross-correlations given traditional architectures, where the computational demand increases exponentially with the number of antennas involved. Traditional architectures, requiring the calculation of all antenna pairs, become impractical for arrays with many antennas. The introduction of the FFT-correlator architecture reduces the computational complexity, but its results are valid under narrow assumptions regarding data input. Real-world interferometers, where the antenna configurations change over time, no longer meet these criteria, necessitating a new method to efficiently calculate correlations. We propose an innovative approach, where we apply the FFT-correlator by first transforming the antenna data into a common reference frame, common sky frame, and common time frame. By doing so, we successfully calculated the cross-correlations of the Square Kilometer Array's prototype using an innovative transformation scheme that reduces the computational complexity, recovering the full data range in the Fourier domain.

For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for in-depth portfolio analysis but it places an excessive focus on understanding market uncertainty, failing to prioritize trend prediction. While researchers have applied generative adversarial networks and their variants to generate financial time series and analyze their properties, these models are limited in their ability to accurately capture complex multi-factor trends in financial markets. A new study explores the use of multi-task learning with variational autoencoders to model both the behavior of observed financial variables and the distribution of hidden risk factors driving these trends. By combining this approach with Markowitz's portfolio theory, the proposed method enables a more thorough trend prediction and portfolio optimization, outperforming previous methods in both aspects. Notably, the proposed model excels in predicting the direction of trends and identifying the most relevant risk factors, which is particularly important for portfolio analysis and risk management in modern finance.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ in QCD up to three-loop order for all $N$ using an extension of Ibánez-Quevedo's conjecture, involving a symbolic computation with the symbolic summation package MATHEMATICA, for even $N$ in single and double precision, and for odd $N$ in double precision, also validating some previous results for specific integer values of $N$ obtained through the moment expansion by Schneider. Furthermore, for $N$ up to 5, we have calculated the finite parts of the massive QCD massive vacuum polarization functions $A_{1,i}(N)$ and the gluon form factor $C_{F}^{(3)}(N)$ (also denoted $A_{\pi}(N)$ for $i=1$ for $N$ up to 7 in single and double precision.

A groundbreaking method using Bayesian neural networks enhances the accuracy of classifying gamma-ray sources. The study focuses on identifying Fermi-LAT blazar candidates, consisting of BL Lacertae objects and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars. A training dataset is constructed by selecting eligible candidates based on the Gamma Catalogue of Optically Identified CGOIC sources. Analysis reveals that neural network classifications are more reliable, especially in distinguishing susceptible BL Lacertae objects. A thorough evaluation of the neural network's performance involves examining the dataset's distribution and evaluating the prediction results using the Brier score and extension of the BL Lacertae classification work to the FSRC category. A comprehensive dataset and open-source code are provided for further research.

Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users, 
despite available solutions that aim to reduce this form of exclusion. Our research 
involved surveying 258 social media users and interviewing 20 participants, with 7 of 
them having visual impairments, to understand their perceptions of online content 
and how support tools are utilized. Our analysis of the results reveals that 
platforms' efforts are inadequate, and that mainstream users often aren't aware 
of accessibility features. By exploring the broader implications of this 
discoveries, we suggest new approaches for enhancing accessibility and increasing 
user awareness, including incorporating more human-centered storytelling in 
accessible computing.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to generating hypergraphs randomly, which can be viewed as extensions of the standard model used to study graphs. A novel concept called the tensor join is introduced, allowing us to create hypergraphs based on tensors. Utilizing this concept, we develop a method to count the number of hypergraphs generated by a given tensor, which can be applied to study several problems within the context of bipartite graph matching. Additionally, we extend the hypergraph model by introducing a new concept called the multi-part tensor join, using which we create a new class of hypergraphs randomly and study their properties.

India achieved a groundbreaking success with the deployment and functioning of its initial space observatory, AstroSat, and must leverage its achievements and the knowledge gained to significantly increase the nation's involvement in space astronomy worldwide. The Indian Space Research Organisation issued a request for proposals and in collaboration with the Indian Institute of Space Sciences Education, a detailed study was conducted to figure out the requirements for a new telescope. The study resulted in the proposal for the INdian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope, a 3-meter telescope featuring a large diameter, and with numerous scientific instruments providing capabilities in spectroscopy and imaging at the cutting-edge. The INSIST will emphasis on observing the ultraviolet spectrum, and in conjunction with the AstroSat's instruments, it will offer extended spectral coverage. The observatory will be equipped with the ability to monitor time variations in the vicinity of astronomical sources, and it will support research in various fields including star birth and death, the formation of planateary systems, active galaxies and their interactions with cosmos, and the exploration of the interstellar medium. The project has made considerable progress, and the design requirements and physical models for the telescope have been defined in this document along with the potential for future scientific outcomes and their impact on space research.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, the mixed model repeated measures approach often dominates. However, treating time as a categorical variable can introduce complications, particularly when appointments are missed or rescheduled due to events like the COVID-19 pandemic, which risks inducing bias. To address this limitation, a novel method employing natural cubic splines is presented to model time as a continuous variable and utilize treatment effect variations over time. The proposed method exhibits excellent performance in simulations, outshining established methods, including the BAT model. Additionally, a systematic review of recent literature on time-based modeling in Alzheimer's treatment analysis is provided, followed by an examination of its potential using data from BDNF BAE 282 trials.

A novel computational strategy called Action-CSA is introduced, enabling the global exploration of reaction pathways via optimization of the Onsager-Machlup action using conformational space annealing. Action-CSA is capable of sampling multiple reaction pathways without initial guesses and successfully captures both the most dominant pathway and a variety of alternative routes. Pathway diversity is maintained through a crossover operation, facilitating the identification of multiple pathway families. Action-CSA is benchmarked using crystallin and ferredoxin systems, successfully identifying the dominant reaction pathway and generating family pathways. Notably, Action-CSA identifies the dominant reaction pathway even when the system is trapped in a metastable state, highlighting its robustness and effectiveness.

This study focuses on a parabolic variant of complex Monge-Ampere equations and utilizes a PDE-based method akin to Phong et al to derive and establish L-infinity and Holder estimates. Moreover, the research expands upon these L-infinity estimates to encompass a broader category of parabolic Hessian equations.

Building on Church encodings in typed lambda-calculi, we plan to develop a new
framework based on automata theory that relates to the study of implicit
computational complexity, much like how monadic second-order logic connects to
descriptive complexity. We will focus on transductions – functions mapping
strings to strings or trees to trees – particularly those with high growth
rates, including polyregular functions and other complex mappings. To lay the
groundwork for this framework, we have achieved key results that demonstrate
certain transduction classes can be represented using lambda-calculi, offering
insights into a long-standing open problem about simply typed lambda-calculus.
Moreover, we have developed a method to encode regular functions in a version of
lambda-calculus called elementary affine lambda-calculus, which was initially
designed for this specific context, also allowing us to capture a larger subset
of polyregular functions by adjusting our approach.

This concise note establishes a relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flow components are involved in the integrands, with the 'correction' term requiring consideration of Lions-type measure derivatives to determine necessary cross-correlations. It positions this framework in the context of SDEs influenced by conditional measure flows, with the special case being obvious under complete measure flows.

This research aims to investigate various types of normal subgroups using a specific topology derived from hull-kernel-type topological spaces. We have made significant contributions by introducing a new class of normal subgroups known as primitive subgroups, examining topological properties such as separation, compactness, connectedness, and continuity in these spaces. Furthermore, our study paves the way for identifying spectral spaces among these subgroups.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two re-ranking approaches based on column descriptions are presented to mitigate the broadness issue. Experimental outcomes confirm the significance of relevant columns and value filling in cross-domain parsing, and showcase the superiority of our re-ranking methods. To facilitate future research, the dataset and code for this study are publicly available.

In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating while avoiding potential collisions between robots is a significant challenge, largely due to the unpredictable movements of fellow robots. To tackle this, our method develops a data-driven strategy where each robot continually resolves a short-term optimization issue that incorporates safety restrictions based on an optimized risk analysis of close encounters between the agent and other robots. This optimized risk analysis ensures robustness against potential prediction inaccuracies by considering various possibilities and using observed data collected during execution to estimate likely outcomes. By leveraging duality theory from a specific optimization technique, our method transforms this analysis into a computationally feasible approach that applies broadly across distributed and decentralized scenarios, showcasing its value through an experiment involving drones navigating a virtual environment.

Recent data for the Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxy And XXV challenges a previous report of negligible dark matter content. Our research significantly reduces uncertainties by doubling the number of studied member stars. And XXV now shows a distinct dark matter component with mass constrained by velocity dispersion measurements within the galaxy's half-light radius. Our findings reveal a mass-to-light ratio and a metallicity consistent with previously constrained values. Notably, estimating the mass of And XXV's central region results in marginally significant constraints on its cusp slope, indicating a strong need for higher-precision velocity measurements. Furthermore, our analysis yields a scaled mass consistent with a cusp-like slope but due to binary perturbations, the significance of this result is largely attributed to limited sampling of its velocity dispersion. Our model exhibits a remarkably accurate prediction of And XXV's luminosity distribution, shedding light on its unusual shape as influenced by a prominent tidal feature and weak dark matter slope. Our detailed model now enables straightforward extension of its light curve and mass dynamics in various scenarios, such as at different radii or ages. Our results strongly suggest that And XXV's mass will continue to experience a gradual decline in the future.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal grant-free access with low signaling overhead. This research proposes a novel two-stage approach using a genetic algorithm (GA) to achieve low-latency grant-free random access in mMTC systems. Initially, the algorithm identifies optimal guard period lengths to minimize access latency in the uplink. Subsequently, it determines latency-aware transmission time intervals for individual users that maximize a predetermined Q-function. This allows random access with a high probability of successful transmission at the base station. The approach involves a two-stage framework: one resolves for optimal guard period lengths to minimize access latency, while the other determines optimal transmission time intervals based on those guard periods. Furthermore, the introduction of a latency pool quantizer and an algorithm initializer enhance the accuracy and robustness of the genetic algorithm, enabling efficient implementation. The proposed approach demonstrates superior performance in both Q-function and latency criteria, surpassing existing baseline methods.

A few approaches to model the thermodynamic behavior of moist air rely on approximations that can lead to inconsistencies in accordance with the 1st and 2nd laws of thermodynamics. A new strategy has emerged that aims to eliminate these inconsistencies by leveraging thermodynamic potentials derived from their natural variables. In this paper, this strategy is applied to both exact thermodynamic descriptions of moist air and two widely utilized simplifications: the fixed $\kappa$ approximation and the approximation based on dry heat capacities. Notably, a consistent $\kappa$ approximation yields a novel dynamical representation that relies solely on total mass and not on water forms when expressed using virtual potential temperature $\theta_v$. Furthermore, a vast majority of numerical weather prediction models employ the approximation based on dry heat capacities, and converting it to a consistent form yields interesting insights into its underlying assumptions. For instance, this form reveals a new aspect of that approximation, specifically that it implicitly assumes that both water forms of air are in thermodynamic equilibrium with each other and with dry air. As a result, we develop a refined version of that approximation, and we discuss the potential of implementing both the strategy presented in this study and the refined version of the $\kappa$ approximation in numerical weather prediction models.

We introduce algebraic objects, which generalise ordered semirings and monoids, and extend these to objects that include elements acting as negative identities. An exterior algebra analogue is proposed, which provides a cryptomorphism for matroids, and shows that standard exterior and idempotent exterior algebras can be derived from it under specific conditions.

Research on spoken dialogue systems has typically relied on a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses for interpreting meaning and monitoring the dialogue flow.  Nevertheless, confusion networks (a more complex set of possible outcomes than a shortlist) can be a compact representation of the potential outcomes of the system.  We investigate in this study the advantages of using confusion networks with the aid of the most up-to-date neural system designed to follow dialogue (a dialogue state tracker) - specifically one model known as the GLAD model.  We have developed an approach that translates the confusion network into a probabilistic distribution of the different possible dialogue states, and we have found that utilising the confusion network yields improvements of up to 4% accuracy over the baseline in the GLAD model.

We have computed enumerative invariants of semistable coherent sheaves on a complex projective curve, specifically on $\mathcal{M}_{1,\mathbb{C}}[0,0]$. This was done using the method of remote invariants in moduli spaces of p-divisible groups, which mirrors the behavior of moduli spaces of vector bundles. Consequently, the fundamental classes of moduli spaces of vector bundles and (semi)stable sheaves are expressible in terms of Mobius functions, facilitating the expression of Mobius functions without requiring additional calculations. Furthermore, the invariants of pure sheaves on $\mathcal{M}_{1,\mathbb{C}}[0,0]$ coincide with those of Drinfeld modules, enabling the derivation of enumerative invariants of ordinary and over-ordinary character twists of $\mathcal{M}_{1,\mathbb{C}}[0,0]$. Similarly, similar results have been obtained for curve weights. The findings connect the enumerative geometry of pure sheaves to the function field analog of Kontsevich's theorem and its over-ordinary twist extension.

A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified subsets, known as the access structure γ. This study focuses on the most extreme form of access structure, where the number of minimal qualified subsets is either one or two. It's known as the universal access structure and can be denoted as either (1,γ) or (m,m'), where m and m' represent the smallest and largest number of minimal qualified subsets respectively.

The researchers presented a family of secret sharing schemes for any number of participants, including an exhaustive access structure with n-1 minimal qualified subsets for n participants, where n is equal to or greater than 3. They demonstrated that access structures with n-1 minimal subsets are the exclusive outcomes of an exhaustive access structure. A generic protocol was introduced to share a secret among n participants, using two shared secrets, one shared by all participants and the other shared by all minimal qualified subsets. 

In the study, the term "minimal qualified subset" refers to a group with the smallest subset of participants who can learn or reveal shared secrets. An important aspect of the access structure γ is its minimal qualified subset count, while an "monotonically increasing function" refers to a function that can't decrease in value. 

The researchers proved that access structures with n-1 minimal subsets are the only possible outcomes of an exhaustive access structure. They further showed that all known access structures, including (6,7) and (7,8), satisfy the condition of having

To determine entanglement in polarization qubit pairs, we utilize quantum estimation theory to develop the most precise estimators possible, which are found to be compatible with existing experimental techniques. We then introduce a coupled tomography approach that enables optimal precision in measuring entanglement in polarization qubit pairs, specifically pairs of qubits with various types of polarization entanglement, such as the Bell state and the mixed singlet state. Furthermore, the proposed coupled tomography approach is demonstrated to be effective in generating experimental protocols for estimating the densities of multiple qubit systems, specifically two qubit systems. In our study, we focus on implementing the coupled tomography approach using photonic methods and develop a related algorithm to translate density matrix bonds into experimental settings. This algorithm is specifically designed for use in photonic systems and is demonstrated to be capable of producing realistic experimental protocols that are feasible and realizable.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternative explanation, positing that these modes originate from within the edge plasma itself. A closer examination of the modes reveals that they are characterized by localized structures that carry current in the same direction as the magnetic field, and that cause associated plasma shifts in the same direction - a phenomenon also seen in other forms of plasma turbulence. A model has been developed which demonstrates that these modes can be understood as a combination of two distinct magnetic field eddies that rotate in opposite directions and exhibit symmetrical behaviour across the direction of the magnetic field. These modes have been observed to appear simultaneously with the formation of a mode caused by ergodic magnetic field fluctuations that often triggers the PTM, suggesting a possible link between the two phenomena - although the primary source of these modes remains uncertain.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted experiments using both the conventional freezing of pre-trained models and the baseline methods. The results showed that freezing the pre-trained network in conjunction with linear evaluations achieves comparable results (up to 97.5% accuracy on the Split-CIFAR100 benchmark) to sophisticated continual learning methods, including methods incorporating memory and task-adaptive mechanisms. In addition, we discovered that applying l2 regularization in the training process significantly improves the performance of the pre-trained feature extractor in new tasks.

As social media increasingly influences public perceptions globally, researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened social divisions and violent crimes. Previous studies have employed automated hate speech detection methods, but they often fall short by overlooking broader social and contextual nuances. Furthermore, few attempts have been made to explore the explainability of such models, given the gravely damaging effects of hate speech. In response, our framework, AI for Every Thing (AIEt), leverages natural language generative models, grounded in cognitive linguistics, to incorporate contextual understanding. By doing so, we enhance the model's capacity to produce detailed, linguistically fluent explanations for its hate speech classification. In addition to outperforming existing models in classifying hate speech in both English and German contexts, our approach provides qualitative, human-friendly explanations that could potentially inspire human-based interventions. AIEt's generative capacity also facilitates its potential adaptation to other languages, prototypical domains, and pithy text formats, offering a highly versatile system.

We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons.

Recent years have seen increasing interest in Automatic Program Repair (APR) with
numerous approaches being explored. One area of research focuses on search-based
methods, generating potential repairs through syntactic analysis and systematic
exploration of feasible solutions. Conversely, we investigate an innovative
approach inspired by the concept of bugs and repairs from a adversarial
perspective. By utilizing deep learning architectures, specifically Generative
Adversarial Networks (GANs), we are able to produce repairs closely resembling
those generated by humans. Initial evaluations suggest that our approach is
yielding positive outcomes, with a significant proportion of bugs (21.3% out of 500)
 repaired identically to human corrections.

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel with interconnected user pairs, characterized by a collection of interconnected rectangles, with each rectangle defined by paired rates of mutual information. While the full region cannot be exactly computed due to computational limitations, we obtain an inner and an outer bond that converge to an inner and an outer solid, with the inner solid strictly containing the outer solid. Additionally, as a by-product, we find that the width of the outer solid, which represents spectral inf-mutual information rates, equals the direct interference gain and scales logarithmically with the number of users, whereas the width of the inner solid, which equals the spectral inf-hybrid information rates, scales polynomially with the number of users. We employ an alternating optimization method to compute the inner solid, with each iteration being an optimal problem. Specifically, at each step, we fix the transmission rates of all users except one, which encodes the interference-free messages of the other users at a fixed signal-to-noise ratio, resulting in a single-user interference channel. Consequently, we can compute the hybrid information rates of this intermediate channel, allowing us to find the next transmission rate point along the inner solid.

We aim to broaden the established flow analysis technique, which typically operates within the $p_x$-$p_y$ plane, by introducing flow coefficients based on the angular distributions within the $p_x$-$p_z$ and $p_y$-$p_z$ planes. Introducing new flow coefficients, denoted $u_n$ and $w_n$, in conjunction with $v_n$, reveals these parameters are highly responsive to a nuclear substance's equation-of-state. Utilizing $u_n$ and $w_n$, in conjunction with $v_n$, enables the thorough examination of an equation-of-state beyond what $v_n$ can facilitate, making this novel method a more refined tool for investigating the open issue of nuclear equation-of-state in collision experiments. Moreover, our study also shows the joint use of $u_n$ and $w_n$ in combination with $v_n$ permits the exploration of the spin-isotropic degree of nuclear sensitivity to its equation-of-state. In a comparative study, we discovered that the systematic trend identified in $v_n$ vanishes when examining $u_n$ and $w_n$, suggesting that the $u_n$ and $w_n$ coefficients are not susceptible to the anisotropic flow generated by collective motion effects, thereby enhancing their sensitivity to the equation-of-state of a nuclear system. The timely detection of COVID-19 remains a significant research priority, offering potential advantages in the initial assessment and management of suspected patients, while also reducing hospital workloads during the ongoing pandemic. Research into coronavirus detection via clinical data has involved the application of diverse machine learning methods using data such as blood test results and vital signs. However, risks associated with these methods, including data overfitting and limitations in explaining decisions, cannot be disregarded. Furthermore, healthcare professionals and researchers require easy access to explainable models to build trust with patients during the detection process. Although white-box AI models can provide interpretability for COVID-19 diagnosis, these models often rely on limited annotations and suffer from overfitting issues. Therefore, developing robust, generalizable models with seamless explainability is crucial for detecting COVID-19. This study offers ANAIS, an advanced COVID-19 detection model based on ANN, which uses diverse input data and output clear-eyed explanations linking predictors to outcomes. Furthermore, our results reveal that ANAIS surpasses other neural networks supporting explainability on different metrics when using multiple types of patient data.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the robustness of GNN predictions. To overcome this limitation, we develop methods to assess the robustness of decentralized GNN predictions in various wireless communication systems, measuring their resilience against errors caused by interference, irregular data arrival, and faulty nodes. We then experimentally validate the proposed approaches via a NodeRNN framework and observe that, in many cases, error correction methods yield superior performance, albeit at increased computational costs. Notably, in some scenarios, a robustness-boundary property emerges, where certain systems can maintain highly accurate predictions despite extreme levels of noise. Based on these findings, we provide guidelines for choosing suitable systems and robustness measures to achieve optimal results in real-world applications.

The threat of homicide death tolls has raised concerns worldwide and demands attention from researchers and government officials, a trend exemplified by the high numbers in Brazil, where homicides have become the primary cause of death for people in the 15-39 age group and the third overall leading cause of death.  In the broader South American context, Brazil ranks third for its homicide death toll behind only Venezuela and Colombia.  In assessing the consequences of violent acts, an analysis of two distinct databases - the Brazilian Public Security Index and the Atlas of Violent Death Data - reveals important variations in homicide statistics by state.  For instance, the state of CearA has the highest homicide rate while the state of AmapA has the highest total count of homicides, highlighting the importance of accounting for differential trends when implementing policy measures to address this issue.

Our goal is to obtain a precise, probabilistic estimate of the iteration step count needed to achieve a given level of approximation for a wide class of non-convex optimization problems, including those that may not meet certain regularity criteria. To this end, we begin by revisiting two established optimization algorithms, stochastic gradient descent with diminishing step sizes (for strongly convex functions) and stochastic gradient descent with dampening (for smooth, convex functions), and adapt them for non-convex optimization problems. We utilize sharp probabilistic bounds on performance estimates to derive rigorous results for a general class of iterative algorithms, including the usual methods, without regularization. These findings indicate that one can obtain a precise step count estimate by averaging the usual upper bounds on algorithm performance. For example, one can obtain a convergence rate of $O(1/k)$ for minimizing non-convex, smooth functions using stochastic gradient descent with diminishing step sizes, and $O(1/k^2)$ for minimizing non-convex, smooth functions using stochastic gradient descent with dampening. Additionally, we derive a convergence rate of $O(1/k^{3/2})$ for minimizing non-convex, strongly convex functions using stochastic gradient descent with diminishing step sizes. We also derive a convergence rate of $O(1/k)$ for minimizing non-convex, smooth functions using the interior point method. These results have the advantage of being applicable for a wide range of functional optimization problems, including those that may not meet certain

Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, the leading explanation for the strong-CP issue.  Variants of axions known as axion-like particles (ALPs) also arise in various modifications of the Standard Model, particularly in string theories.  Both axions and ALPs have compelling justifications as potential components of Dark Matter (DM), and substantial quantities would be generated at the Sun's core. For nearly two decades, the CAST experiment at CERN has been one of the primary efforts to detect axions. The IAXO project, an upgraded version of CAST, is well-suited to explore axion halos, specifically those found in the Earth's rotation through the rotator mechanism, in addition to continuing the search for ALP halos using the rotator mechanism. The IAXO experiment will also enhance efforts to detect ALP halos by significantly boosting sensitivity to these particles, and will be able to detect axion-derived DM through "axion rain" diffusion, and will be capable of detecting ALP-derived DM through halo-related diffusion. The IAXO project will be capable of detecting ALP-derived DM through halo-related diffusion, and will be competitive with other detection methods such as the "dark disc" method aimed at detecting DM derived from decaying ALPs.

The occupation number over time is examined for a bosonic oscillator coupled to heat baths with fermionic and bosonic components. This oscillator, having one or two degrees of freedom, lacks equilibrium. Such a system serves as a means to establish dynamic non-stationary memory. It has also been established that this type of system is analogous to well-documented nonlinear self-oscillating systems.

Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex challenge. In comparison to other object-grasping fields, dexterous grasping has been understudied, mainly due to a shortage of extensive datasets. To address this issue, our study introduces DexGraspNet - a large-scale simulated dataset - designed specifically for robotic dexterous grasping, aiming to aid dexterous grasping research acceleration. Unlike existing datasets, which often neglect critical elements, DexGraspNet incorporates a diverse range of factors, including diverse end-effector poses, oriented objects, and grounded 3D-pointclouds. Utilizing advanced computer-aided design tools, our dataset features highly realistic and visually appealing 3D-object models. In contrast to other approaches, our method employs a single model to generate diverse end-effector poses, which are then paired with realistic grasps based on these positions. Additionally, our method employs a combination of noise functions to create various object orientations and pointclouds. In an effort to ensure that training data effectively leads to optimal performance, we carefully examined the distribution of successful grasps within DexGraspNet. Specifically, our method employs a Gaussian distribution to sample end-effector poses, which are then evaluated against a collection of strongly grasped objects. Furthermore, our method closely resembles human hand movement, and pointclouds are sampled based on the distance between the center of the object and the center of the hand. Importantly,

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy guidance, particularly for diagnosing and treating abdominal and thoracic diseases or tumors. To rectify respiratory movement issues, a novel technique involving temporary data concealment and subsequent compensation via a respiratory-gating technique is developed and evaluated. A specific spiral-in-time acquisition method with thin-slice imaging is also used, enabling a short breathing cycle and high temporal resolution. To compensate for respiratory movement, a novel T2-weighted 4D-MRI sequence with multi-slice imaging is developed, incorporating data from concealed and respiratory-gated 1D-MRI sequences. A computer simulation is used to assess and compare the MRI signals of a multi-slice imaging model with those of a single-slice imaging model under respiratory-gating using the normalized mean square error and correlation coefficient metrics. To validate the simulation results, MRI scans of two healthy human subjects were conducted, revealing that the multi-slice imaging model exhibits better slice separation than the single-slice imaging model, with notable improvements in slice thickness difference of up to 1.25 times and slice spacing difference of up to 0.64 mm in the first subject, and up to 1.35 times and 0.64 mm in the second subject. Consequently, a new, high-quality 4D-MRI sequence with multi-slice imaging and respiratory motion compensation is developed,

We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100.

Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and their respective level set foliations are examined. The equivalence of these functions topologically implies the topological equivalence of their foliations. Conversely, this relationship is not always valid; however, we define a specific class of functions, denoted by (A), for which the converse holds true. Members of class (A) are functionally defined as being closely related to two-variable polynomial equations, where at least one variable's influence is present. The closedness of this class is demonstrated through various inclusion relationships, showing that the class of submersions, denoted by (S), along with other subclasses (C) and (T), are all contained within (A). The paper concludes by establishing a specific topological equivalence relationship between submersions, but only for functions in class (S).

Ecosystems that naturally thrive in dry environments have become increasingly vulnerable due to the rising threats of degradation and declining productivity. One notable aspect of these ecosystems is the spontaneous formation of plant patterns that can visually appeal and help regulate their response to stress. Research has shown that herbivory is a critical mechanism behind the creation of these patterns and the functioning of the entire ecosystem. Despite this, many mathematical models that analyze the interaction between grazing animals and plant growth often neglect the role of spatial distribution by considering the mean grazing effect across the entire area. In contrast, an approach employing partial differential equations captures the dynamic relationship between plants and grazing animals, incorporating the influence of spatial distribution. By applying this framework to a simple model, this study examines the impact of homogeneous and heterogeneous vegetation on dry-land ecosystems, revealing that systems with uneven vegetation can better resist stress and maintain their resilience.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches.

A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its implementation on central and graphical processing units and interfacing with PySCF. Preliminary timing benchmarks compared to existing C++ codes show ipie performs equally well or better on both CPUs and GPUs. AFQMC results for the isomerization of [Cu$_2$O$_2$$]^{2+} and the association of LiF pair also demonstrate accurate energies. AFQMC results for the binding energy of the LiF pair and the association dissociation energy of the HeH molecule were also shown, providing a benchmark for wavefunction-based methods.

High-frequency trading could greatly benefit from first-generation quasi-quantum communication technologies. This text outlines a simplified game-theoretic approach using the two-player game known as Prisoner's Dilemma. It examines how quasi-quantum communication can expedite transactions in the Fourier sampling category, specifically in the case of random variables. The results demonstrate the potential for substantial time savings in Fourier sampling via quasi-quantum communication during high-frequency trading, with significant time reductions achievable - regardless of the number of trials. This finding suggests that quasi-quantum communication could provide a valuable advantage of at least an order of magnitude in the case of high-frequency trading across all Fourier sampling applications. The approach described could also underlie a new approach to multi-agent learning across all fields where agent interactions can be represented through game theory, while potentially laying foundational groundwork for the development of new quantum algorithms in economics.

We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-value buyers with private valuations that follow a distribution $F$ for each buyer. 

When the items are identical, we develop a design of incentive-compatible auctions for any $k$. 

When the items are distinct but have similar characteristics, we develop a class of short and efficient auctions that approximate the optimal social welfare with high probability, using only $O(\log k)$ rounds of interaction and a constant number of messages, independent of the distribution $F$. 

When the items are distinct with unique values, we develop a short and efficient auction that approximates the optimal social welfare with high probability, using only $O(\log k)$ rounds of interaction and a constant number of messages, independently of the distribution $F$. 

All of our designs achieve specific distribution-free guarantees, regardless of the distribution $F$. 

Our approaches combine techniques from top-tournament mechanisms, probabilistic auctions, and directed graphs.

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an efficient planning mechanism that enables the generation of grounded summaries. This method involves pre-annotating summaries with entity sequences that capture key information, and training a transformer model to predict these sequences. At the generation stage, we use the predicted entity sequences to guide the model and ensure that generated summaries contain all crucial details. Experiment results demonstrate that this planning approach leads to significantly improved grounded text summarization, outperforming a baseline in both accuracy and fluency. Additionally, we find that incorporating entity sequences results in more precise summaries, as well as higher semantic consistency.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors, suggesting the importance of understanding entrainment patterns in conversations. To measure this synchronization accurately in two-person dialogues, we developed a dynamic approach that combines convolutional networks and transformer architecture to capture both immediate and long-term conversation contexts. By incorporating attention layers for analyzing both internal and external interactions, our model can learn meaningful patterns in social exchanges across various domains. Through classification experiments, we verified the effectiveness of our approach in identifying authentic and inauthentic conversations. Moreover, when testing our model with individuals having Autism Spectrum Disorder, our results indicate a strong statistical link between our entrainment measure and relevant clinical symptoms, regardless of age and gender differences.

A recent study applied a realizability technique to establish the meaning of a quantum lambda calculus, which results in a multitude of acceptable typing rules, all of equal standing. Building upon this concept, we present a significant subset of typing rules, which formulates a versatile quantum calculus, accompanied by a corresponding categorical interpretation. Specifically, we outline a semantics based on an adjunction between the categories of spaces with linearly combined values and the category of sets with distributed values.

Analytical calculations have been performed for two types of quasiparticle excitation energies per particle in systems of up to seven electrons within both the Laughlin theory and composite fermions theory, accounting for the comprehensive jellium potential consisting of electron-electron, electron-background, and background-background interactions. The findings support that the composite fermions wavefunction outperforms the Laughlin wavefunction in energy for two quasiparticle configurations, albeit the difference in their energies diminishes with growing system size.

In the context of glaciology, particularly for polar ice sheets, Stokes variational inequalities effectively capture inequalities arising from Dirac-Krein transforms and model non-penetration conditions. This research focuses on a numerical approach, introducing a specialized formulation called the $Q$-Variational formulation (QVF) to circumvent the issues associated with stabilisation techniques. A convergent numerical scheme comprising a stabilised discretisation and a QVF method has been developed and implemented on irregular domains with both Raviart-Thomas and Stokes finite elements. The proposed method facilitates the solution of open-boundary problems via the extension of variational inequalities into equalities through the concept of variational inequalities as equalities. This approach enables the efficient computation of ice sheet and shelf combined systems. Numerical simulations demonstrate the method's reliability and efficiency in modelling polar ice sheets.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how
gas moves out from the area where the galaxy is forming new stars. Our data show a powerful
outflow of gas, moving at 460 km/s, within the area where the galaxy's core is located. The
mass flowing out of the area is much higher than the rate at which the galaxy is creating new
stars, nearly 10 times higher. This outflow of gas is moving at a high speed, nearly 800
km/s, outside of the area where the galaxy's core is located. Our data show that the mass
flowing out of the area is growing as we look further away from the area, increasing by a
factor of 3. The model we used, based on NOEMA data at different times, shows that the
outflow of gas is moving rapidly, moving several hundred parsecs in just 5 years. Our
data also reveal two areas of moving gas, one in the area where the galaxy's core is located
and one outside of it, seeing the gas moving in the direction of the galaxy's movement in
space at the same time. The mass moving in this type of movement pattern
is much lower then what we see in the area where the galaxy's core is located. Our
findings indicate that the gas moving out of the area where the galaxy's core is located
is causing the gas to leave the area

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\varepsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\varepsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

In our research, a novel, straightforward technique is introduced to synchronize robot movements within digital simulations and physical tests, utilizing a centralized broadcast method. This approach, dubbed Black Box Broadcast, functions similarly to a traditional black box method but eliminates the need for a specific contract, achieving synchronization of robots based solely on provided instructions. Additionally, a specific broadcast method called Multicast BB has been implemented using a car navigation system across multiple wireless connections. Testing of this approach demonstrated its effectiveness in attaining exact synchronization of robots, even in the presence of delayed data arrival. These results demonstrate that Black Box Broadcast offers an efficient solution for attaining high-precision timing synchronization in complex robotic systems.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so it's highly desirable to leverage datasets with annotated labels as much as
possible. Unfortunately, there aren't many large datasets for segmentation,
although there are plenty of unlabeled videos available. Our work investigates
whether depth estimation can be a cost-effective way to develop a deep network
capable of segmentation tasks as well. We selected three prominent depth
estimation architectures and revealed through our experiments that one of them
produces significantly better results than the others on benchmark datasets,
notably KITTI. Moreover, it outperforms networks trained with labeled data and
exceeds even the current state-of-the-art models designed specifically for
segmentation tasks.

Let's consider the set of all analytic functions defined within the unit disk in the complex plane and have their absolute value strictly less than one, denoted by the symbol. The classical Bohr's inequality deals with a power series that converges in the same unit disk, and we can derive that its terms satisfy the inequality for a certain fixed constant where. The function representing this fixed constant is known as the Bohr radius, and we can obtain an improved radius under certain conditions, particularly in the context of log-harmonic mappings. These mappings belong to a set that satisfies a non-linear partial differential equation with a harmonic coefficient, and we can obtain further results by considering a subclass where such functions preserve the original direction of an arrow with respect to their starting point within the complex unit disk.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is explored, along with an efficient method for estimating its value from data. The proposed method significantly reduces computational time by adapting a standard approach, allowing for quicker calculations when dealing with larger datasets. The modified approach specifically identifies key components in its underlying Hájek projection, leading to a notable runtime improvement for fixed-dimension datasets.

The number of connected devices has seen tremendous growth, creating vast volumes of diverse data that intertwine with our physical world. The Edge Intelligence System has emerged to harness edge computing and AI, facilitating intelligent services through powerful processing and near-instant decision-making. With increased autonomy at the edge, concerns about data security and privacy have become more prominent, necessitating a shift in the paradigm of intelligent services towards ones that are more private. By leveraging edge computing's distributed architecture, we can create hybrid models that integrate local and remote machine learning to reduce data transmission and safeguard user data. However, training machine learning models on incomplete datasets at the edge poses significant challenges. In the context of intelligent transportation systems, edge computing can enable efficient and fast decision-making for vehicles, especially when dealing with time-critical applications like lane detection. This work proposes an advanced lane detection framework that combines deep learning model training on both the edge and remote servers, utilizing a semi-supervised approach with both semi-supervised and supervised learning methodologies. The framework incorporates a novel triangle-based asynchronous method using the Message Passing Interface for parallel execution on multiple platforms. The results demonstrate the success of this approach in accurately identifying lanes from images captured by cameras simulating advancement behind obstacles.

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical and computational feasibility of the Euler characteristic make it an attractive intermediate step for multi-variable topological analysis. We demonstrate its practicality by using artificial datasets and a real-world example involving diabetic retinopathy detection from retinal images.

Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model based on Holling-Tanner's equations with a Type II predation response, added with an Allee effect affecting prey, influencing their coexistence, extinction risks, and cycles. We extend previous studies by incorporating this adjusted Allee effect into Tanner-Holling's equations to understand its effects on model behavior. Certain parameter combinations lead to the existence of stable limit cycles, while others result in stable fixed-point solutions, demonstrating a significant role of the Allee effect in determining the long-term survival or extinction of the species.

The Hirsch Conjecture was a theory claiming that a d-dimensional polytope with n faces cannot exceed a diameter of n - d. This assumption was contested by Santos, whose findings led to the conclusion that some linear programming methods cannot perform optimally within n - d iterations. This series of research was initiated by a novel algorithm, the facet pivot method, proposed in the first paper. This second paper verifies the efficacy of the facet pivot method, confirming it can solve linear programming problems in at most n - d iterations, motivated by Smale's mathematical problem 9, and building upon Polyak's alternative formulation of the simplex algorithm.

We explore in an associative ring R with identity, the scarcity of k-torsion in the NK1GQ(R), which are Bass nil-groups for general and unitary quadratic groups. Building upon a graded version of Quillen-Suslin theory, we establish an analogous concept for graded rings.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the extensive computing requirements for precise particle physics calculations at Colliders, specifically the Large Hadron Collider. Beyond the standard model, complex scenarios such as multiple beyond the standard model particle productions via various processes like gluon fusion, electrogluon fusion, and electroweak corrections, require off-shell and non-resonant contributions. To facilitate this comparison, the study designs and evaluates a software framework named JUJU, based on the Java programming language, aiming to produce accurate results in line with the benchmark results obtained from the parallel computer program CHANEL. The study further enhances JUJU by incorporating numerical libraries with64-bit precision and using the software to predict various beyond the standard model particle properties such as masses, decay widths, and couplings.

The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent presentations restricts their adoption in high-stakes applications. Effective countermeasures against these deceptive attempts are vital for the safe integration of facial recognition technology. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. In this research, transfer learning is applied from the vision transformer model to tackle the challenge of detecting unknown anti-spoofing attacks. Experimental results conducted on widely accessible datasets showcase the superiority of our proposed solution, outperforming state-of-the-art methods significantly in zero-shot scenarios within the HQ-WMCA and SiW-M datasets, while also achieving substantial improvements in cross-database evaluations.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for modeling complex behaviors and interactions.  Despite initial hurdles in fine-tuning its algorithms for more realistic scenarios, recent advancements have made LSTMs a key component in successful applications such as game playing, natural language processing, and speech recognition.  However, the field of machine learning still faces challenges in developing intelligent systems that learn from examples automatically.  To explore the potential of deep learning in developing safe and intelligent self-driving cars, we employed a successful reinforcement learning framework developed by Volodymyr Mnih and colleagues and adapted it for use in simulating autonomous vehicle behaviors.  Our results show that using example-based learning can successfully predict the outcomes of vehicle behaviors on roads, both locally and remotely.  Moreover, we found that using simulation-based training, combined with real-world road-scene data for fine-tuning, can result in robust and generalizable vehicle control policies when predicting road conditions becomes challenging during actual driving.  Our approach does not rely on specialized hardware, as our software-based system for vehicle behavior modeling and learning can function on standard laptops and is compatible with multiple software versions.

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs). However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes after each solution evaluation. As APEAs provide a higher chance of selection to quicker solutions, the evaluation speed bias negatively affects the overall search performance. In an effort to address this drawback, a novel parent selection technique has been proposed to minimize the idle time and improve efficiency. Results from our experiments have shown that the new approach not only reduces idle time but also achieves better performance compared to existing methods across various optimization problems. Moreover, our selected scheduling strategy also exhibits robustness when faced with frequent computational communication delays, ensuring superior overall performance.

The recent microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 involved a cold super-Earth planet located among a group of eleven planets where the mass of the host star compared to its planetary mass is under ten thousand, providing valuable insights that are relevant to understanding the origins of both the mass variations and relationships among these planetary systems. OGLE-2017-BLG-1434's icy planet has a mass equivalent to 1.07 times that of the Earth and orbits a 0.75 solar mass host star, located 5700 parsecs away. Upon analysis, this planet's mass and the mass of its host star are found to be at a significant point in a mass variation power law. This power law displays distinct behaviors based on whether the mass of the host star is high ($M_{*} \gtrsim 0.6 M_{\odot}$) or low ($M_{*} < 0.6 M_{\odot}$), showing that for planets with masses no more than 10 times that of the Earth, the majority will be part of systems with masses no higher than the solar mass. This power law also shows that for planets with masses no more than 10 times that of the Earth, the majority will be part of systems with mass ratios no more than ten thousand, providing valuable insights to the underlying causes of the mass variations among these planetary systems. The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods and often obtained through analytical high-frequency expansions. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a Markovian master equation of the Lindblad type, poses a significant challenge. In systems with only two energy levels, distinct phases arise, including a regime where the Floquet generator is non-Hermitian and gives rise to exponential growth of decay rates. We provide an explicit high-frequency expansion of the Lindblad generator, enabling a deeper understanding of these phenomena and offering a framework for future simulations in multi-level systems.

Our recent studies of the effects of Rh content in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ reveal the emergence of magnetic irreversibilities and spin freezing in the vicinity of x ≈ 0.6, accompanied by a suppression of long-range ferromagnetism. Through detailed analysis of the temperature and field histories, we observed pronounced evidence of long-range ferromagnetism at lower concentrations (x < 0.6) and pronounced spin freezing at higher concentrations (x ≥ 0.6). Furthermore, long-range ferromagnetism can be successfully reinstated in the higher concentration regime by using slower cooling rates. We suggest that the unique characteristics of the Rh-rich system, including the presence of additional phase transitions, may be responsible for the observed spin freezing, which is unlike the behavior of the rhodium-free system.

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope, 19-beam tracking has successfully observed high sensitivity and velocity resolution spectral lines from hydrogen (HI) toward a massive star-forming area, G174+29.8. The goal of this research was to identify HI narrow-line self-absorption (HINSA) toward regions where CO absorption is present, specifically within the areas of high-mass star-forming regions and regions of galaxy interactions. The research utilized a novel technique to correct for phase delays by calibrating spectral scaling and obtained results that demonstrated excellent uniformity across all bands with a 1 sigma error of approximately 0.8 millikelvin. The research data revealed uniform sensitivity across all bands with a 1 sigma error of approximately 0.8 millikelvin. The research data showed that the flux density of the calibrator source 3C286 accurately reflected its known flux density, specifically 2.87 Jansky, with minimal errors. The research data also revealed a high correlation coefficient of 0.99, indicating accuracy in the cross-scanning and phase switching patterns. The research data further demonstrated an average noise level of approximately 1 millikelvin. The research data successfully detected HI narrow-line self-absorption (HINSA) toward the test areas, specifically within the areas of high-mass star-forming regions and regions of galaxy interactions. We demonstrate the topological equivalence, under topological entropy preservation, between a class of beta-transformations with holes within the interval (0,1) and their corresponding greedy beta-transformations also featuring a hole in the same interval, both of which fall under the category of piecewise linear expanding maps. By establishing this connection, it becomes possible to derive additional insights from the study of greedy beta-transformations, thereby providing novel topological and dynamical results for beta-transformations with holes. In addition, this allows us to address and provide answers to an open question proposed by Hoffman and Kra, which involves exploring the occurrence of factors of the form $(x_0,x_1)$ on beta-transformations, with it being shown that such factors can indeed exist. Moreover, this study's findings also uncover new aspects of renewing sets, particularly those associated with greedy beta-transformations, as well as offering a different and potentially more tractable approach to investigating the occurrence of overlaps between Rauzy graphs, which was also highlighted by Hoffman and Kra.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics sources. Utilizing approximately 7,421 +/- 105 signal events from predominantly CP-odd final states (J/\psi pi+ pi-), which were isolated in about 8.2 x 10^4 mixed events, researchers performed a time-dependent analysis on early LHC data from the CMS experiment. With the help of a model-independent fit, they found phi_s to be -0.019 +/- 0.137 radians, in line with the Standard Model predictions. Further analysis revealed no indication of direct CP violation. Furthermore, further studies on the angular distributions of the decay products in the states (J/\psi phi) and (J/\psi K+ K-) may lead to discoveries in the future, given increased statistics.

It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from a given dataset, but they may not necessarily excel in adapting these features to datasets with different underlying characteristics. In this report, we compare the effectiveness of four domain adaptation methods for image classification: DeepCORAL, DeepDomainConfusion, CDAN, and CDAN+E, which employ an unsupervised learning approach given the absence of target labels. Our analysis of these methods is performed using the office-31 dataset, with a GitHub repository detailing the report available at: https://github.com/agrija9/Deep-Unsupervised-Domain-Adaptation.

To determine the total number of such arcs, a specific counting method, called hypergraph containers, is used to establish an upper limit on the total number of arcs, represented by $A(q)$. For small values of q, specifically for prime numbers or powers of 2, we calculate the exact total number of arcs, while for these cases we find that the established upper limit on the total number of arcs, $A(q)$, is accurate.
