A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+1}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+1\}$ and non-degenerate triangles formed from the vertices of this triangle, noting that it excludes the possibility of forming equilateral triangles when $n<3$. We then extend this result to all types of regular polygons.

Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph structures and node attributes) to understand model predictions, but generating comprehensive explanations is an intractable problem due to computational constraints. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the concept of explanation templates to allow for the generation of explainable explanations at explainable time complexity. Our approach is evaluated on diverse GNN models, benchmark learnable explanation datasets, and real-world applications, demonstrating its efficacy and efficiency.

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its development and composition, we examined archival X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, examining the dynamic cluster state and searching for evidence of gas mixing. Its X-ray brightness distribution exhibits complex movement and tension, identified as primarily driven by a south-east to north-west oriented shock with elevated surface brightness, located $\sim$ 0.37 degrees from the axis and corresponding to a 65 degree angle. We calculated the shock's movement speed at $\sim$ 1025 km/s, indicating the cluster is developing through a cool core formation process. Furthermore, a cluster filament in the north-west sector showed signs of gentle curvature, pointing to a moderate level of gas mixing. The presence of a cool core in this cluster challenges the theory that cooling cores are rare at high $z$. Additionally, it raises questions about replacing core formation by quenching as the primary method for explaining the disappearance of cooling cores with increasing $z$.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was developed and has demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets. In this work, the linear component of the LMU is optimized, resulting in a simplified variant that can be trained in parallel, thus overcoming the obstacle of GPU training limitations on RNNs. Our modification allows training to proceed up to 200 times faster. Furthermore, the performance of our model is evaluated on seven benchmarks in comparison to the original LMU and several other prominent deep networks. Our models consistently achieve superior results on these datasets and, in many cases, are parameter-efficient, achieving a new benchmark result on psMNIST and surpassing the original LMU accuracy on K41, IMDB, and CIFAR10 by a substantial margin.

As the next decade unfolds, the field of particle physics is driven to unravel the enigma of dark matter, the universe's imbalance of matter over antimatter, the seemingly calculated balance of the electro-weak scale, and various fundamental physics aspects.  A significant new research frontier has arisen, involving new, low-mass physics, below the GeV scale, with extremely weak interaction strength, equivalent to a fraction of the strength exhibited by neutrinos.  In pursuit of this, experiments with unprecedented sensitivity are being designed, capable of detecting particles that interact only fractionally with matter, such as dark matter or sterile neutrinos, which may be components of dark matter.  Some theories even suggest that such particles could exist at higher energy levels within early universe "reechoes" of fundamental physics processes.  A global network, the low-mass electron neutrino community, has been formed.  Within the United States, the LENS and SubLENS consortia have been formed to develop deep underground experiments designed to identify evidence of new, feebly interacting particles.  As part of this, the SENSEI experiment at the Large Underground Xenon (LUX) Lab will utilize high-sensitivity germanium detectors to identify the signature of $\sim$10 keV particles interacting with electron-rich xenon targets.  In this work, the motivation, physics case, and prospects for these experiments and others are outlined, as well as their goals and projected limitations in terms of sensitivity.

Language plays a vital role in a culture's fabric, deeply intertwined with human migration patterns. Investigating migration dynamics through the travel of individuals and the spread of languages helps reveal the underlying mechanisms guiding migration. A theoretical framework describing migration can be translated into rules governing the movement of individuals, and we explore the consequences of implementing random migration in a circular landscape. Random migration leads to the widespread dispersal of individuals and populations, and we observe that migration does not result in the formation of distinct linguistic isolates even when languages become fixed over time. Conversely, migration does cause the fragmentation of languages and formation of linguistic isolates when languages evolve over time. Additionally, our research examines the effects of different migration patterns on language dispersion and the formation of linguistic isolates.

PINN algorithms have made significant breakthroughs in solving various complex PDE-based problems. Despite these achievements, they often struggle to achieve optimal convergence when the target function contains intricate details. By leveraging the properties of neural tangent kernels, we have developed a method to analyze the behavior of PINNs. Our theoretical findings reveal that these algorithms may not converge optimally when the target function contains high-level features, depending on the network's architecture. Notably, our investigation seems to contradict the common practice of increasing network complexity by widening rather than deepening the neural network. Based on this understanding, we recommend constructing PINNs with multiple layers, rather than a single layer. Moreover, our theorems suggest that incorporating more data points, rather than increasing the network's width, is an effective way to enhance convergence. To validate our theoretical observations, we conducted various numerical experiments, examining the influence of network design on the solution accuracy of diverse high-dimensional PDEs. Our findings from these experiments support our theoretical predictions, highlighting the importance of carefully designing PINN architectures to achieve optimal performance.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave absorbs energy and the other does not, with partial damping that mimics a viscoelastic material's behavior. Prior research showed that with damping throughout the entire domain, the system's energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Using the frequency domain method in this paper, we demonstrate the system's behavior changes significantly due to the waves being coupled and the non-smooth damping coefficient, specifically that it loses its rapid exponential stability and instead experiences a slowing decay at a rate no better than $t^{-\frac{1}{12}}$.

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread applications in various domains, yet deep RL methods exhibit two primary limitations: efficiency and transparency issues. High-dimensional observational data often necessitates deep models to represent complex information, leading to computational demands and search problems. Moreover, the use of deep models hinders transparency and understanding of their decision-making processes. To address these concerns, this paper employs mixture models for state and action representation, thereby substituting deep models in RL applications. We develop a novel RL framework, called the State Action Programmed mixture model (SAPm), which integrates maximum likelihood estimation with reinforcement learning goals. SAPm is evaluated in synthetic, robotic, and video game environments, successfully achieving efficient and transparent performance in all test scenarios.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even at telecommunication wavelengths, exemplified by designing a quasi-circulator with a 200.5 MHz 3-dB bandwidth. Additionally, we've observed high isolation levels, up to 40.8 dB, between countersinking ports. We've also demonstrated the capability to control the flow of light through specific resonators using weak optical control fields, achieving isolation ratios exceeding 20 dB. Furthermore, we've observed the nonreciprocal effects of field enhancement, both for circulators and diodes, with a notable field enhancement of 16.2 times for circulators and a 10 times for diodes. We've also applied classical coherent light to tune and switch the resonator gaps, showcasing their capabilities. This technique enables the construction of optical devices with extremely small isolation levels and field enhancements, opening possibilities for future applications.

We expand upon the research initiated by P. Fenton by analyzing a function that sums translates, defined as F(x,t):= J(t) + Σ[n from j=1] ν_j * K(t - x_j), where the function J maps the interval [0,1] to the real numbers including negative infinity and is sufficiently non-degenerate and bounded above. Additionally, the kernel function K maps the interval [-1,1] to the real numbers including negative infinity and is concave on both the intervals (-1,0) and (0,1). Given a set of positive values ν_j and an n-element vector x with 0 ≤ x1 ≤ … ≤ xn ≤ 1, we investigate the properties of local maxima in the function F, including their behavior across translations and the set of points x, and demonstrate the sufficiency of a specific condition involving the function J, the vector x, and the values ν_j, in relation to the function's behavior on the interval [0,1].

The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for directly detecting dark matter particles. Offering a broad spectrum of research opportunities, from measurements in moles of rocks to individual crystals, its approach is versatile and effective. Using a combination of low-thermalized fidility targets and cryogenic temperature heating measurement, CRESST is capable of detecting very light dark matter particles directly or through mediation by target nuclei through coherent scattering. Additionally, CRESST can investigate the ionization signal produced by these mediating particles exclusively in the target containing the fidility material. This experimental technique has been highly effective in generating some of the strictest constraints on the interaction between dark matter and nucleons, particularly for interactions with nucleon-averaged strengths above $10^{-22}~\mathrm{cm}^2$. Recent updates to the experiment include significant improvements in detector sensitivity, primarily an 8-fold enhancement in individual crystal mass, new read-out techniques that offer improved spatial resolution, location selection, and energy threshold at 2/100 keV. All these advancements have been successfully tested in the experiment's off-shoot demonstration phase at the LNGS laboratory in Italy. CRESST's upcoming third phase, featuring an 80 kg science mass featuring light targets and cryogenic calorimeters, is poised to take leading position among direct detection experiments. This development offers particular opportunities for the experiment to produce notable results on the interaction between dark matter and electrons, particularly for masses less than an GeV. Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, parameters of which are derived from a latent image's variably blurred variants. Current research relies on parametric models for deblurring, which are insufficient in capturing the diversity of real-world blurs. In this research, we introduce a nonparametric model based on kernel mixtures for blurs and develop a robust optimization method to resolve a poorly defined problem. The model can naturally handle a range of blurs and, when applicable, effectively reduces to parametric models, accurately capturing task details. Our algorithm's convergence and accuracy are theoretically validated through synthetic and real-world tests, demonstrating superior performance.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant BiHom-bialgebra with quasitriangular properties and show that the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation of weight -1 can be derived from a unitary quasitriangular covariant BiHom-bialgebra. Lastly, we outline two methods for constructing BiHom-pre-Lie modules from Rota-Baxter paired modules.

Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for assessing and
ensuring correctness in software, covering a range of abstract program
behaviors. Despite its usefulness, Hoare logic faces challenges in processing complex programs due to exponential complexities in proof construction, resulting in impractical proof processes and tool performance limitations for high-level programs and automated proof methods. To address these limitations, we examine strategies for significantly speeding up Hoare logic proofs, focusing on program transformation techniques that enable the reduction of proof complexity, the separation of concerns allowing reasoners to tackle specific sub-problems independently, and the aggregation of overlapping proof hints from multiple specialists.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol, however, assumes a pseudo-random network topology in its design and lacks a formal consensus definition, limiting its application to pseudo-random networks. This work expands the traditional Canopus algorithm to accommodate non-pseudo-random networks, introduces a definition for consensus, and formalizes it while guaranteeing similar time complexity and energy efficiency as its predecessor.

Recent studies utilizing neutron spin correlation experiments have delved into the elastic properties of lipid bilayers, with particular focus on the impact of cholesterol. The findings show that cholesterol decreases the bending modulus of lipid bilayers composed of palmitoyl oleate phosphatidylcholine (POPC), thereby facilitating membrane curvature. An earlier computer simulation by Venable et al. attributed this effect to cholesterol's ability to reduce interleaflet pair correlations, thus increasing the membrane's curvature-favoring content. Contrary to this hypothesis, our research indicates that cholesterol actually enhances, rather than diminishes, the interactions between lipid headgroups and interleaflet lipid pairs. The effects of cholesterol on lipid bilayers, particularly the altered interactions between lipid A and fatty acid chains, complicate the existing understanding and discourage reliance on simplified computer models that simulate lipid membranes.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its modified Friedmann equation is analogous to that of the APS LQC model. Notably, the model's critical matter density at the bounce point is a quarter of the original APS LQC model's, with the critical density $\rho_{cL}$ equalling $\frac{\rho_{c}}{4}$. This discovery implies that quantum gravity effects will manifest earlier than previously thought and also make detection potentially easier due to a lower critical density.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made available 
for close examination, alongside nine events used to establish the energy scale 
for each detected primary particle. An accompanying plot displays the locations 
where these energetic particles entered Earth's atmosphere, leaving their data unmarked 
for scientific investigation. Furthermore, the presented analysis examines how 
these energetic particles correlate with nearby active and inactive galactic 
nuclei, spanning a 75 Mpc radius, exhibiting striking alignments with AGN W.lyrae 
and AGN NGC 1068, and also examining correlations with the GW event 190428, a 
supernova remnant, and cosmic strings, while keeping silent on these particular 
astrophysical phenomena.

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions. Researchers have developed uncertainty estimation methods for deep object detectors but encountered difficulties with information loss during non-maximum suppression and the multitasking nature of anchor generation. Our approach builds on the discriminative uncertainty framework and introduces a novel method for uncertainty estimation in deep object detectors. We adapt this method for robotic applications by formulating detection uncertainty as a minimax problem between expected detection accuracy and detection cost. Our experimental results demonstrate improved robustness for uncertainty estimation in detection problems on the COCO dataset and increased detection rate in costly detection situations. Furthermore, we use the developed method for motion planning in an autonomous vehicle navigating through parking simulators at varying levels of imaging quality.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems and public daily life.
The traffic4cast competition pushed the limits of short-term traffic prediction, leveraging high-resolution data from Munich to pinpoint traffic flow.
Entry to this competition involved using the full German Traffic Online (GTO) dataset, but our innovative approach uses patch-based processing to achieve more robust predictions.
Instead of training on the full dataset, we began by training on smaller, locally-corrected patches to improve spatial prediction accuracy.
Similarly, to tackle the complexity of high-resolution images, we trained on overlapping patches to refine our predictions.
Using a data augmentation technique, we incorporated spatially-corrected predictions, leading to improved performance on the training dataset.
The combination of these innovative techniques results in top-tier performance, specifically:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Velocity prediction: 0.698
  \item Count prediction: 0.521
\end{itemize}
The code for this project is open-sourced on the traffic4cast MUNich repository.
The repository utilizes the Lightning JAX framework, allowing for seamless integration with the JAX library.
The use of this framework leads to significant performance increases, specifically:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Velocity prediction: 0.698 ($\times$ 2)
  \item Count prediction: 0.521 ($\times$ 2)
\end{itemize}

In recent years, rewriting theory has been used to create systematic approaches to proving coherence in strict higher categories. We're taking this theory further by applying it to Gray categories, which can be thought of as a specific type of tricategory. To achieve this, we need to adapt rewriting theory to the context of precategories, which encompasses Gray categories, and allows for automated calculations. Our findings demonstrate that precategories with a limited type of structure consisting of one generator and one defining relation are coherent. This result serves as a foundation for understanding the coherence of Gray categories, which we've shown to be equivalent to the coherence of strict 2-categories. Our approach also enables us to calculate the coherence of the composition and 2-m Composition Laws in monoids, which translates to Gray categories.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We have developed and validated an open-source, state-of-the-art deep learning method that uses an extended 2D multi-orientation approach with automatic pre-processing and orientation alignment. We re-created and evaluated the HI-2D multi-orientation approach using a mismatch between training and testing datasets, which resulted in lower accuracy. We further demonstrated that our new approach performs better than the original method when evaluating with different datasets and configurations. Additionally, our new method outperforms existing non-trained deep learning methods in evaluating with epilepsy data, showcasing its potential as a strong baseline model. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of data sharing and the usability of imaging data and code in the medical field.

We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair sharing a path. Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover inconsistencies in the description. By incorporating transversal modes and examining the emergence of correlations in detector positions, we uncover an apparent violation of classical causality. Furthermore, we highlight that individual detector positions cannot accurately pinpoint the correlation between pairs of detectors. Instead, a metric based on overlap between weak values from detectors provides a more reliable measure of such correlations.

Our research identifies the Arctic Circle landscape as an ideal location to study the mechanisms creating the inner proton radiation belt. An experiment was set up at an altitude of approximately 500 meters above ground level, using two parallel scintillator detectors to track proton trajectories. By reproducing the conditions of Earth's polar region, the experiment aimed to clarify the primary mechanisms behind proton radiation belt formation. An analysis of the data revealed that proton radiation belt creation is primarily the result of betatron radiation accompanied by some contributions from proton-proton collisions.

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This 
paper proposes a novel three-phase training approach based on expressivity 
criteria, consisting of global model reduction, weight refinement, and weight 
redistribution among links. In the first phase, we reduce the model's size 
using a previously developed criterion, in contrast to others which utilize 
practical considerations. Subsequently, we refine the weights according to a 
criterion that distinguishes between classes, and finally, we re-distribute 
weights between links for hard-sample training. The three-phase approach, 
in conjunction with a data augmentation technique, outperforms state-of-the-art 
methods, notably DenseNet, and highlights the significance of expressivity in 
designing efficient models for different application domains, particularly 
those with limited data.

To protect user data in matrix completion services, we consider a privacy case where each entry is independently masked using either original or artificially modified values. We develop an algorithm for this setting by integrating a matrix completion method with an optimization technique inspired by the iterative hard thresholding algorithm. This approach is influenced by the work of Lui et al. (2022), who applied a different optimization technique to a similar problem, although our framework is more broad and also applies to the case where users provide incomplete data. Our method resolves an optimization problem that combines data reconstruction and privacy, using the Huber loss function to balance optimization efficiency with accuracy. Numerical results demonstrate that our approach consistently achieves a better balance than the Tikhonov regularization technique on various tasks and datasets, while also improving reconstruction precision.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a paucular mixture of refractory materials. This mixture includes materials that are highly refractory such as silicates and carbonates but poorly represented by standard grain compositions, and materials such as PAHs that are highly refractory and have been detected through their absorption and emission spectra. PAHs are known to be largest in regions of active star formation and are largest in the diffuse ISM in Carina. Applying the PAH model to the diffuse ISM in Carina we find that PAHs account for approximately 25% of the total dust, a value in line with the results of other authors, and in conjunction with other dust components result in a best fit composition that matches the dust properties observed in the far ultraviolet and far infrared bands. Our results confirm that PAHs are a significant component of the ISM and should be modelled as individual molecules to avoid their spectral properties being predicted by the thermal emission from small graphite grains.

Research into exoplanets has led to groundbreaking discoveries surrounding low-mass stars, including the identification of giant planets in binary systems and the detection of candidate planets around the smallest known stars in the universe. Assuming that the formation processes of planets are similar for low-mass stars, we analyzed data from the AGPM instrument at the CFHT to observe potential planets around the low-mass stars VLMB1 and VLMB2, both of which are thought to be single stars with estimated masses of 0.13 and 0.09 solar masses. The AGPM instrument, equipped with its 1880 mm^2 detection zone, is one of the most sensitive planet-detecting devices, enabling the detection of planets as small as 2 M_E at 123 pc. The AGPM observed VLMB1 and VLMB2 in the infrared during which it took 126 images of the region to observe the stars, over a period of time of about 5 hours. The process of the data involved the elimination of three relevant U band photometry from the dataset of VLMB1 and VLMB2 showing them to be stable and constant in their measurements. The elimination of the flux variability left the possibility of planets with the minimum mass of 0.5 and 0.3 the mass of Jupiter in order to not have the photometric data deviate. The data also shows the possibility of planets with an orbital period of 5.83 and 2.71 days in the case

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching board game played on a given graph, where players make moves in rounds by turning off as many on lights as possible.  A starting configuration of lights will be referred to as 'irreducible' if no player can turn off all the lights by only turning off off lights. A key result in this area, proved by Cohen, Kuipers, Kuipers, and Sullivan, states that for any graph, there exists an irreducible configuration that can be turned off in 2n-2 rounds on a set of n lights. This result notably includes bipartite graphs and initially seemed to provide an alternate proof for a conjecture made by Bollobas and Sanders. A follow-up result by Cohen, Kuipers, and Sullivan stated that for any graph, when using rounds in a '1-2' sequence (either turning off all lights or turning off lights), there exists an irreducible configuration that can be turned off in at most 2n rounds on a set of n lights. This result notably includes bipartite graphs and was conjectured to include hypergraphs. A generalization of the '1-2' sequence was explored by Frieze and Zelevinsky who proved that for any graph, it can be turned off in at most 2n rounds and also off in at most 2n rounds. This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed approach to effectively handle images with significant noise or artifacts. Notably, in medical fields, images may be distorted by noise or microscopy artifacts, which the proposed model can effectively address. The framework can also be leveraged to enhance the accuracy of image segmentation tasks in mixed-cell populations, even when the identities of individual cells are not clearly defined. Extensive experiments and simulations validate the efficacy of the proposed model in various scenarios.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily switching from an initial approximation to a more precise one, before applying the interpolation phase to improve overall accuracy. The proposed approach is theoretically justified and tested on a simple case study, which yielded substantial gains in precision for several different scenarios.

A wide range of topological phonons has been theoretically predicted to exist in materials exhibiting specific symmetry properties. We successfully isolated topological phonons in manganese phosphorus and strontium silicon, compounds that can be either hexagonal or orthorhombic in shape. The detailed phononic behavior of these materials was demonstrated through both the real-space representation of atomic motions and their frequency spectra. Furthermore, any potential instability of the atomic structure due to phonon oscillations was evaluated using the elastic constant method. Our findings suggest manganese phosphorus and strontium silicon represent promising candidates for further investigation into their phononic properties.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their minimal data requirements. However, traditional distance-based approaches often trade accuracy for data assumption-free operations, making them less effective in general situations. In order to address this issue, a new outlier detection method is proposed, combining the advantages of assumption-free distances and accurate results from nearest neighbor ratings. The proposed method utilizes an efficient data structure to rate data points based on their nearest neighbors' distances, providing both efficient computation and reliable outcomes. Moreover, incorporating a balancing parameter allows users to rate data points either locally or globally, depending on the specific needs of their application.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus when it's at rest. Comparing these scenarios shows that the enhanced emission probability induced by motion doesn't depend on the type of boundary conditions imposed behind the plane.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate in local neighborhoods. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is built on two core components - the first enables the construction of equitable neighborhoods for any node in a graph and the second allows adaptation to accommodate specific data constraints. Notably, while numerous studies have explored link fairness, understanding of neighborhood fairness remains limited. In our work, we introduce novel measures of fairness centered around node-level neighborhoods and demonstrate their relevance through three data constraints. Furthermore, we develop algorithmic solutions to achieve neighborhood fairness, first by establishing a fair neighborhood for any given node and subsequently adapting to accommodate specific data constraints. Our extensive experiments on seven diverse datasets showcase the effectiveness of our method, and highlight the significance of neighborhood fairness in the context of inductive representation learning.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the applicability of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to non-linear equations. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive accurate and efficient analytical solutions to non-linear reaction equations. By transforming non-linear equations into simpler linear forms, these methods enable the derivation of accurate analytical solutions that align well with both exact solutions and the results of numerical methods. Furthermore, the convergence of the solutions obtained through these methods is validated, demonstrating that approximate solutions can effectively approach exact solutions as the number of iterations increases.

Theoretical physicists conduct experiments in final stages with data obtained from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Direct detection of squarks and gluino is challenging due to squarks and gluinos decaying into hidden states of neutralinos and LSPs. In squark and gluino decays, there are masses above 2 TeV for squarks and 2.5 TeV for gluino that result in virtual states resulting in missing energy. In such an scenario, searches for events with high energy jets and vanishing energy are performed. Assuming the presence of $\Delta \chi$ states in gluino decays, then gluino mass as 3.5 TeV becomes accessible in current stage of experiments. In such an scenario, searches for events with high energy jets and vanishing energy are performed by postulating the presence of $\Delta \chi$ states in gluino decays. Furthermore, effective field theory at masses as 3 TeV for delta-chargino and 3.5 TeV for delta-neutralino reveals new physics at these masses, and thus these masses become the lower bounds through finite threshold effective theory at these masses, and thus these masses become the lower bounds through finite threshold effective theory at these masses, and thus these masses become the lower bounds through finite threshold effective theory at these masses.

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble collapse can be marked by an explosive growth in prices that suddenly ends at a potential critical point. The varied predictions among rational individuals make it difficult for them to unanimously decide on the correct market price once it deviates from its fundamental value, thus facilitating the emergence and survival of financial bubbles. The exponential growth in prices is linked to a rapid increase in market activity as key individuals exercise their options to sell at increasingly overpriced market conditions. The exponential growth can be halted at its theoretical critical point if enough market participants start selling, yet this is prevented in our models by the selling being initiated at a time lag due to varying expectations among individuals. The models also show that the actual market price closely follows an expected pattern of fundamental value, price, price-squared, price-cubed, etc., with the constant term being the most significant, thus explaining observed multi-stage patterns in financial data.

Quantum harmonic oscillator solutions are derived, considering a semi-infinite simple pendulum and a quantum system remaining still, coming into contact with a classical harmonic oscillator, with the latter's general properties substituted for its amplitude and angular frequency. Utilizing the oscillator's zero-energy states and treating the pendulum as nonrotating, solutions are found for a quantum system connecting to its classical limit, as well as one that always oscillates, thus never reaching the classical limit.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the existing approaches have focused solely on predicting user ratings rather than their overall preferences. In contrast, predicting multi-class preferences is a more accurate reflection of user behavior, especially when it comes to recommending multiple items. To address this gap, our work proposes a novel approach that analyzes sentiment to improve the prediction of user preferences across multiple items. This is achieved by first developing a sentiment analysis model that accurately captures the underlying sentiment of user reviews. Next, our work utilizes the sentiment analysis results in two different ways: a deep model that predicts user preferences and a maximum likelihood model that predicts ratings. To support our approach, our experiments demonstrate significant improvements over baseline models on multiple real-world datasets, resulting in a notable increase of at least 8% in accuracy for predicting top 8 recommendations. Overall, our work highlights the significant benefits of combining sentiment analysis with rating prediction.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into enhancing the utilization of data from both monolingual and mixed languages to create a cross-language model through the development of a novel approach using CLML, the Canadian French and Malay language. The objective is to create a singular, unified model rather than independent ones for each language. The enhanced cross-language model delivers better results compared to the baseline model on both language tasks: translation and classification. Furthermore, the study includes an analysis of a locally created dataset consisting of CS texts from two local websites.

We will demonstrate that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group- and coset-spaces, which generalize the lambda-deformation phenomenon. Utilizing a sigma-model approach, we found that all the established conformal brane geometries in the context of products of WZW models satisfy the relevant boundary conditions, thereby maintaining their integrability across the relevant renormalization group flow. Our results encompass various known cases as special instances, and we're also exploring new discoveries in this area, such as the recently introduced Faulkner geometries.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across domains, including engineering and computer graphics. A fundamental concept in addressing these challenges is the mesh, a composite of basic elements where hexahedral units offer enhanced computational advantages. However, mesh integrity relies on the quality of its components. The issue arises when elements take on shapes hindering precise calculations, rendering them unusable. To deliver accurate outcomes, it is crucial to correct such elements' morphology, rendering them valid. This study synthesizes the outcomes of two studies to develop a mesh assessment and correction framework. By combining their findings, we establish a functioning algorithm but also recognize its potential for enhancement, thus introducing multiple improvements to accelerate its processing speed and adaptability. The resulting method is then demonstrated with real-world applications, showcasing its applications and displaying its output.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably high precision, demonstrating an average error of less than 2% across an extensive range of technological parameters and output loads. As a result, the proposed model presents itself as a computationally efficient solution for diverse technology nodes and probabilistic gate delay characterisation applications.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
equipping your model with accuracy and precision, especially when considering the
potential for varied outcomes. In the realm of reinforcement learning, attributing
a precise quality score, or Q-function, to each environmental state can aid in
guiding actions towards better outcomes. Fostering a Q-function that accurately
scores states, especially in environments that rarely return to similar states, can
be challenging. In the context of continuous states and actions, we address this issue by
limiting the rate of change in a model's quality scoring system, effectively
imposing boundaries that aid in finding relevant solutions. By encoding this scoring
system as a neural network, we demonstrate its effectiveness on challenging games, as
well as its transferability to similar games, demonstrating its potential in
facilitating Federal agents when applicable and safe agent decision making in
general.

The underlying mechanisms behind the ventral temporal cortex's animacy detection remain poorly understood. We hypothesize that the animacy continuum is explained by either the Primate Visual Hierarchy or by Simpler Neural Causality. To test our hypothesis, we conducted an experiment that tested the predictions of both theories and found that the results from anatomical connectivity align more closely with the Simpler Neural Causality model. We also reevaluated the empirical evidence in the field and concluded that the majority of it is more consistent with the SNCC model. Our findings contribute to the growing debate about how the animacy continuum in VTC is organized.

In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world conditions is a top priority. However, commonly used methods such as the finite element method and finite volume method are often prone to inaccuracies and artifacts, like Gibbs oscillations, particularly when approximating complex characteristics. This necessitates an efficient and accurate approach that can effectively address inconsistencies like negative concentrations or temperatures at a reasonable computational cost. Our study focuses on a novel numerical technique, the projected finite difference method, which combines projected elemental methods with standard finite difference approaches. By leveraging the capabilities of projected methods, the projected finite difference method is able to ensure the satisfaction of fundamental constraints, while also allowing for the incorporation of additional constraints via Lagrange multipliers. Our results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in solving various problem classes, including the heat equation, the Poisson equation, and the advection equation, in both their linear and nonlinear forms.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. The data includes 25 observations with an interval of $\le$0.1 days. In hard-intermediate states, QPOs were detected at frequencies of 1.22, 1.41, and 1.54 Hz. Combinations of correlation analysis and fast Fourier transform were used to validate the results. Furthermore, a high-cutoff blackbody model was applied, revealing an interval of 2.42-4.94 days for the light curve of a cental engine size, as well as an unweighted mean size of 3.97 days, and an integrated size of 4.94 days with uncertainty.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' behaviors rather than truly reacting to their actions. To address this issue, we developed an innovative framework for interacting agents using a multi-round message-passing system that allows beliefs about other agents' behaviors to influence decision-making. Unlike previous MARL methods, our approach focuses on learning beliefs about other agents' behaviors rather than the environment. Through the use of variational beliefs and communicative actions, our framework enables agents to make decisions and receive training without needing access to partner policies or communication assumptions. In our setting, agent beliefs serve as a central memory, allowing decisions to be made and receiving training without needing partner policies or communication assumptions. In our evaluation on the classic game of Guessing Game, our framework outperformed existing MARL methods by achieving significantly better performance and avoiding brittleness, even in settings involving highly uncertain partner behaviors.

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and 
approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and 
transferring similarities and transitions across materials and textures. 
MatSim features a diverse range of fuel-resistant film materials, 
carefully arranged in various quantitative and qualitative configurations, 
along with corresponding ground truth data and practical applications in 
real-life scenarios. Our goal in developing MatSim involves leveraging 
computer vision capabilities to quickly identify and simulate material 
transitions or similarities across materials and textures. To utilize 
MatSim, users can apply existing computer vision techniques, such as 
classification or segmentation, on top of our generated datasets. 
Experimental results are provided for both full and sparse targeted 
applications. Moreover, we present two novel applications - one for 
automatically arranging objects and another for transforming simulations 
in a physics engine - to showcase the practical uses of MatSim. 
Ultimately, MatSim aims to bridge the gap between existing computer 
material recognition tools and novel human-like capabilities for 
experiencing and simulating the sensations and reactions of various 
materials and textures.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by introducing four different types of Lie 2-algebras derived from 2-plectic manifolds, Courant algebroids, homotopy Poisson manifolds and multivector fields on a Lie groupoid. The Lie 2-algebra cohomology is also reintroduced and its lower-degree instances analyzed. The integration of strict Lie 2-algebras to strict Lie 2-groups is also a point of discussion in the paper.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we leverage self and cross attention mechanisms in the Transformer model to derive feature descriptors that are context-dependent for both images. This approach allows our method, known as LoFTR, to effectively find dense matches in low-texture regions where traditional detectors face difficulties. Experiment results on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods with significant margin and excels on visual localization tasks, topping rankings on two prominent benchmarks.

The paper addresses concerns surrounding the influence of Faraday rotation measures (RMs) on the determination of magnetic field components. Specifically, we focus on the bias that can arise in measuring magnetic fields perpendicular to the line-of-sight due to RMs. We determine that the biased component is the square root of a measured value. We identify local screen, hybrid, and volume screen models as the primary causes of biased measurements. We select the simplest screen model, mixing screen, to investigate the phenomenon further. We establish the relationship between the ratio of magnetic fields and the mixing angle, and develop equations for predicting bias. Through numerical analysis, we explore the behavior of bias under varying parameters. We find that the bias can be considerable, and becomes more pronounced at high signal-to-noise ratios. We conclude that the phenomenon is more pronounced at high frequencies, and suggest the use of polarization angles to mitigate the bias.

This research paper explores a real-world example that demonstrates the effectiveness of real-time pricing in reducing peak-hour electricity demand. We collectively refer to peak-hour pricing schemes, peak-load shaping schemes, and peak-demand pricing schemes as real-time pricing (RTP). Consumers are becoming increasingly aware of the benefits of RTP due to its potential to shift their energy consumption from peak hours when power supply is scarce and usage costs are higher, to off-peak hours where rates are lower and supply is more abundant. We humanely employed RFID technology to implement RTP in public charging stations for Electric Vehicles, while ensuring that stations remained operational under various scenarios. Our approach involved designing an efficient system to record vehicle arrival and departure times, estimating battery levels and energy consumption during peak hours, and adjusting RTP parameters to maintain a suitable level of electric charge demand. Experimental findings show that the proposed system effectively encourages consumers to move their energy consumption from peak hours to off-peak hours, thereby optimizing total energy costs and reducing peak-hour demand on power plants.

The generalized form of the Einstein theory, the Rastall theory of gravity, incorporates the law of conservation of energy and momentum. We derive a charged black string solution using the Newman-Janis approach in a Rastall theory background. Next, we investigate thermodynamic properties, such as Hawking temperature, for these black strings and study their graphical representations with respect to event horizons. Additionally, we examine the impact of Rastall theory on Hawking temperature and assess the charged black string stability. Furthermore, taking quantum gravity effects into account, we investigate modified Hawking temperatures. We also explore the physical behavior of these black strings in the presence of quantum gravity and a spin parameter stemming from the Rastall theory.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of time-averaged observables in the asymptotic regime can be described through series truncations, and these results are illustrated with the example of a transverse field Ising model at criticality. Similarly, the results can also be applied to Schrodinger operators with discrete spectra.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. These stars are rare, and only five have been detected with a metal content below -5.0 so far; moreover, determining their birth locations is a challenging task for these primitive stars. Recent discoveries, including an iron-poor star with a content of -5.45, and another with a content of -4.96 that shares a common ancestor, suggest that the metal-rich population among globular clusters may predate the metal-poor stars observed today. We present the findings of a new metal-poor star, observed using the Keck/ESI spectrum, with a content of -5.06 that resides far from the Galaxy's center, specifically within the outer region of the outer disk. Furthermore, another metal-poor star, observed using the NIRC2 and ESI instruments with a content of -4.6, has been identified, located approximately 0.86 degrees from the Galaxy's center, specifically within the outer disk. Epsilon Chasi effect implies that younger stars within the Galaxy's disk exhibit a lesser variability in metallicity as we move further from the Galaxy's center, specifically in the outer disk region.

This research splits the Earth into a grid of hexagonal cells to collect and analyze worldwide data on daily fire counts from each cell to evaluate seasonal fire severity, defined as accumulated detections per season. The primary aim of this investigation is to assess the accuracy of time series forecasting models using historical active fire data for short and medium-term predictions. This straightforward approach utilizes globally accessible data to facilitate scalable prediction. The study's findings encompass both the methodology's proposed applications and limitations, beginning with an examination of the observed trends in seasonal fire patterns, followed by an evaluation of the theoretical implications of using hexagonal cells in data collection. Furthermore, it compares the performance of machine learning models in predicting fire severity for regions with well-established fire patterns and those considered risky. The analysis also explores the potential of using active fire data for predicting regions with moderate fire risk. The research further delves into predicting fire risk by considering weather and spatial factors using historical and weather data. The prediction outcomes of the employed models demonstrate their adequacy for providing timely decisions in response to fire emergencies.

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our investigation identifies patterns of correlation among them. We compare the methods to a principal component analysis of the data, ultimately finding that several methods approximate the first principal component of the data set. The first principal component appears to reflect the overall level of morphological complexity in the data, much like how the first principal component of exam scores might reflect the overall difficulty of the exam. Consequently, several measures exhibit striking similarity to each other. Moreover, we demonstrate that some methods are statistically equivalent through user studies. The findings suggest that employing multiple measures to assess the same aspect of language is unnecessary, and that single measures can be sufficient.

Researchers at Meneghetti et al. 2022 incorrectly applied an inaccurate, approximate model for self-interacting dark matter substructures. This approximate model contradicts actual numerical simulations of self-interacting dark matter. To correct the issue, our study re-examines observations for individual clusters, utilizing the ADMARE simulations, and shows that self-interacting dark matter is capable of matching observed satellite counts. Conversely, standard cold dark matter is inconsistent with these observations. Self-interacting dark matter substructures have lower density profiles, especially at low radii, and this properties persist in high-density environments. Self-interacting dark matter substructures have lower rotation velocities, especially at low radii, and this properties persist in high-density environments. Given these results, our study re-examines the predictions from ADMARE simulations for galaxy-galaxy lensing and galaxy dynamics in clusters, and finds that self-interacting dark matter is consistent with these predictions, assuming an isotropic cross-section. However, standard cold dark matter is inconsistent with these predictions. This resolution could be further confirmed with future galaxy-galaxy lensing and galaxy dynamics observations in clusters. These results also indicate that self-interacting dark matter, when interacting optimally, can match the observed magneto-spherical acoustic peak height, a finding that contrasts with standard cold dark matter models. This resolution could be further confirmed with future magneto-spherical acoustic peak height observations.
