We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs high-resolution radio-frequency detection. The use of this approach has allowed us to continue experimenting on materials even that have become damaged, providing valuable insights into processes such as island formation and dot-interaction. The long-time stability of this method has also enabled us to study long-time behaviors that would otherwise be inaccessible. Furthermore, the approach has allowed us to distinguish between electron tunneling and alternative non-electrical mechanisms that could also result in the detection of magnetic or photon flux. The approach also allows us to control and analyze the behavior of the island in a superconducting state, enabling us to observe features such as superconductivity, critical levels, pair-breaking, and Asymmetries in tunneling. The use of this approach has also allowed us to explore untested areas of research, including the behavior of superconductors, critical levels, and quantum dots, and the potential applications of tunneling phenomena in superconducting systems.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. To expand upon existing work, we introduce a new metric that can accommodate spatial variations and use it to establish conditions under which shockwaves in a broader class of systems, such as fluid flow equations, will behave predictably. Furthermore, we identify specific criteria that certain types of shockwaves must meet in order to be expected to behave predictably. Our investigation into these conditions includes the 7-equation combustion model and the equations that describe the flow of a binary gas, as well as a broader class of systems, such as an illustrative model, in one dimension.

We explore novel unsupervised techniques for generating detailed 3D scenes from distant vistas, analogous to a futuristic 'fly-through' video production process. Our research indicates that conventional solutions based on GANs are prone to generating less accurate 'hall of mirrors' type scenes, along with resulting training difficulties. In contrast, we demonstrate that diffusion models are more suitable for extended 3D scene extrapolation tasks. Our solution entails conditioning each 3D step with not one but two images: a distant view and a nearby point of interest. This allows our model to efficiently generate detailed scenes while maintaining consistency with distant views. Our approach excels in various evaluations and is made publicly accessible via https://diffusionscapes.com.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the underlying dynamic processes, detecting random complex patterns remains a pressing issue. We develop a new, straightforward method grounded in mathematical techniques to discover and manage complex patterns that arise on large networks, even for datasets lacking information on dynamic processes. This approach identifies underlying dynamics by analyzing diverse patterns simultaneously. We demonstrate its effectiveness in multiple case studies, showing it can uncover a mix of random and predictable patterns within the same network and also restore deleted information with high accuracy.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a proposed method for controlling the film's evolution through the regulation of slip or stick at this interface. The models presented indicate that any deviation from no slip leads to a faster rate of film thinning, which increases exponentially over time, ultimately resulting in instability. Conversely, sticking tends to slow down the thinning process and can make it less likely for the film to become unstable. It is also suggested that an unstable film will always thin faster when stick is favored over slip at specific dynamic interfaces. The models developed relate to specific scenarios such as the breaking of towers into droplets and the evolution of films on long fibers.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two human evaluators measured and compared the coronal image deformity angles acquired from both robotic and manual scans. The results showed that robotic scanning yielded comparable deformity angles to manual scanning, with values close to what was found through clinical measurement. This technique was found to be both reliable and accurate. Furthermore, it was found to be less dependent on user expertise compared to manual scanning.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. It was discovered that models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architectures, a subclass of residual networks, address one of the main limitations of ensemble learning - reduced robustness. Yet, MIMO models are inefficient in resource usage since each input branch contains identical weights, thereby neglecting potential diversity between pathways. Our investigation focuses on mitigating this redundancy and assessing its impact on robustness by adapting MIMO architectures to handle multiple inputs. We propose a novel weight sharing strategy, MIMO with Mosaic Pathways, where inner and skip connections within residual blocks have separate parameter sets, enabling diverse pathways. We then extend MIMO to multi-task problems, introducing a novel gradient aggregation technique that surpasses traditional ensemble methods in performance while significantly reducing resource usage. MIMO achieves a state-of-the-art accuracy of 50.9% on CIFAR-100 and 82.0% on CIFAR-10, demonstrating more robust performance than standard residual networks and ensemble learning. Furthermore, MIMO outperforms competitors on MIMIC and MVTec datasets in multi-task and single-task settings, respectively. Importantly, MIMO significantly surpasses traditional residual networks and ensemble learning in low-data regimes. MIMO's code is publicly available at https://github.com/MimO_MOSAIC/MIMO_MOSASIC.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets relevant to document image analysis, encompassing key tasks such as document layout extraction, identification, translation, and categorization. Upon scrutiny, we observed that the current datasets have significant limitations and only partially address these key tasks. The principal limitation of the existing datasets is that they fail to integrate sufficient information regarding task-specific guidelines and instead rely solely on page-level annotations. The absence of these details leads to difficulties in evaluating recent deep learning approaches designed for document image analysis. In response, we have developed a new benchmarking framework known as the WaNet Dataset Challenge, aimed at addressing this gap. The proposed framework undergoes comprehensive evaluation in this paper, with the view of inspiring future research enhancements. Specifically, we have outlined a step-by-step improvement protocol and suggested possible directions for optimizing document image analysis methods based on the results obtained from the analysis of state-of-the-art techniques in this field.

Despite the widespread use of industrial robots in various applications, their performance is often limited by their lack of precision in positioning and tracking.  Two main causes of deformation are responsible for this in particular machining applications.  To improve the accuracy of robot-based machining systems, we present a novel method for calculating pose corrections.  Our method utilizes an optical data analysis approach to identify and compensate for the effects of deformation.  It does this by capturing the natural movement patterns of robots, reconstructing their frames, and pinpointing the sources of deformation.  Based on empirical research conducted with a diverse group of participants, we developed an algorithm that utilizes averaged pose data to correct system misalignments.  Our experiments indicate that this approach can achieve superior precision, often surpassing traditional deadband-based techniques by as much as two orders of magnitude.  Moreover, we found that this method functionality can be expanded to monitor and detect potential failures in real-time.

The study of how chronic diseases and health conditions progress over an individual's lifetime is a focus of research for the medical and economic fields. Advances in statistical analysis have made it possible to examine this phenomenon, which appears to be influenced by both short-term and long-lasting effects of early experiences and specific risk factors. Understanding the patterns and risks involved in health development across a person's lifetime can help identify opportunities for early diagnosis and prevention, ultimately reducing the economic and social impacts of major diseases. Several theoretical models have provided the framework for this line of inquiry, which is being explored through data analysis by the medical and epidemiological fields. The primary goal of this research is to quantify changes in health over a person's lifetime by using longitudinal data from large studies to create persistent health profiles. By applying the principles of Bayesian analysis, which enables the seamless integration of various data sources, the study has investigated how early life experiences, current environmental and social factors, and specific risk behaviors influence health development over a person's lifetime. The research has discovered evidence suggesting persistent patterns in health and lifestyle across a person's lifetime, which have been quantified using hierarchical mixture models. The study has validated these models by identifying distinct groups within the data that exhibit consistent traits lasting decades, which have been found to be associated with early life risk factors, lifestyle choices, and specific health conditions. One effective approach to evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves using Becke's partitioning scheme to break down the integration process into simpler tasks. This method has significant potential for computational modeling of molecules with multiple atoms. Nevertheless, when applied to such molecules, without any additional correction, the scheme often leads to errors in predictions, particularly in cases involving charged molecules or those with multiple charge defects. This response proposes a new correction to address this limitation, which relies on an auxiliary function to modify Becke's partitioning scheme and ensure accuracy in charge-extended molecules. Furthermore, the combined method comprising the MP2 fitting solver and the revised partitioning scheme has been implemented into a software program called PauKar Roothaan. As a demonstration of its capabilities, the new method was applied to calculate the solvent effect on the electronic structure of ribose sugar, using a solvent model consisting of up to 298 water molecules and the generalized Born approximation to simulate the environment's influence.

A graph G is said to have a resolving set if there's at least one subset of vertices where every single vertex in the subset has a distinct set of neighboring vertices. More formally, a subset S from the vertices of G meets the condition that for each vertex v in S, there exists a distinct set of vertices T sub S such that each vertex w in T has a distinct set of neighboring vertices when compared to v. A graph G is said to be resolvable if a resolving set S exists such that every vertex in S directly connects to every other vertex in S and this set is the minimal subset that achieves the resolving property, a property known as being maximal. A resolvable graph is said to be resolvable in the strictest sense if it meets the criteria of being full and this set is the minimal subset that achieves the resolvable property, a property known as being maximal. Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. In contrast to typical cooling effects, 'hothouse' climates are distinguished by a blocked window region for water vapor, which has led to theories of resulting temperature inversions and altered cloud formations. Prior climate modeling has failed to resolve turbulent air motions and cloud dynamics directly, leaving significant gaps in understanding hothouse climate processes. In this research, simulations resolving convection explicitly found that 'hothouse' low atmospheric heating shifts the water cycle from steady state to a periodic regime, characterized by alternating periods of high and low precipitation. The transition to this regime is mediated by changing solar insolation levels, which result in periodic rainfall and cloud formations. Notably, this study has explicitly quantified the rapid heat transfer by turbulent motions in hothouse environments, which has important implications for future climate studies.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel, related theory that encompasses both Yang-Mills theory and its higher-spin equivalents in twistor space.

The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on a vast quantity of high-quality, labeled images which often contains errors. Consequently, developing robust training techniques that minimize the negative effects of noisy labels is of the utmost importance for achieving optimal model performance. We propose an innovative method that utilizes Bayesian statistics to develop self-correcting training and inference procedures for deep neural networks. Notably, this approach can simultaneously identify and correct label errors for individual training samples while determining the probability of error in other samples, making it an optimal solution for datasets with noisy labels and those with limited data. Using specific statistical error models, our approach achieves notable improvements in the accuracy and stability of classification results across multiple challenging datasets, including those in the medical field.

Let $L^p(Q_n)$ denote the space of functions for which the $p$-th absolute mean value when $p < 1$ is finite, and let $\|f\|_{L^{p}(Q_n)}$ represent the function's $L^p$ norm. A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and an explicit formula is given for the characteristic polynomial of the CRW's transition probability matrix, utilising a determinant expression related to the graph's generalized weighted zeta function. This investigation is exemplified through the analysis of regular graphs and semiregular bipartite graphs. Additionally, the CRW is shown to be equivalent to the superposition of independent random walks on specific dynamical schemes, and the CRW's stationary distribution is found to be identical to the Grover walk's stationary distribution.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.

The accuracy of models predicting the spatial arrangement of instantaneously varying wall-shearing-stress patterns in certain fluid flows, specifically those that adhere to a statistical repetition, has been evaluated. A specific focus was given to turbulent channel flows and the 3D structure of shearing stresses along the boundary. It is crucial for models to accurately account for the movement of shearing stresses and the interconnection between the flow's various dimensions, especially at different scales. Comparisons were made between the predictions of various geometrically based models and direct simulations of turbulent flows, taking into consideration the variations that occur at different scales and the consistency of statistical patterns. Results showed that geometrically based models can accurately predict the characteristics of shearing stress patterns for Reynolds numbers that are relatively easy to simulate and can capture both the characteristics of the flow's movement and the interconnection between the flow's dimensions. However, this is especially true for the movement of shearing stress patterns at smaller scales. Additionally, geometrically based models can accurately predict the characteristics of shearing stress patterns in turbulent channels, especially at different scales. This is true without any assumptions or corrections regarding how the movement of shearing stress patterns relates to the movement of the flow's interior. A combination of the geometrically based models and statistical assumptions yielded highly accurate predictions that were in line with the results of direct simulations of turbulent flow characteristics, especially at different scales. This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field behavior. The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an approachable approach to describe self-dual solitons through a variational principle. Ultimately, the study reveals that solitons may arise from non-trivial electric field configurations in the Born-Infeld term while maintaining zero electric flux. With a given Skyrme model lagrangian with multiple parameters, the study shows that both stable and unstable solitons may emerge, characterised by various properties.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has one or more orbital magnetic flux quanta, we calculate the energy levels. The orbital degeneracies are broken by the applied field, creating non-Landau levels. The research shows that each orbital has a set of energy levels that are close to zero, separated by an energy gap. The number of these zero orbital levels scales with $q^2$ if the orbital degeneracy is not affected by the applied field, where $q$ is the quantum number distinguishing the different orbital levels. The total number of these zero orbital levels is $3l^2$ if the orbital degeneracy is affected or $3(lq)^2$ otherwise, where $l$ and $q$ represent the orbital and orbital degeneracy, respectively. An orbital-dependent hopping term contributes to these zero orbital levels by creating a nonzero energy for them. Additionally, at specific orbital levels, all quantum states, including those with $l=0$, have energies that are symmetric about the zero point. This occurs when the orbital hopping term and the quantum number $l$ have certain symmetries. Observations of zero orbital levels, also known as "kinks," are possible in a band diagram by setting certain symmetries for orbital hopping.

This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, consisting of a hybrid silicon nanoring coupled with a localised assembly of quantum dots, which together constitute an efficient source of unidirectional light. By employing an alternative method to conventional top-dye configurations, we have effectively enhanced light interaction between quantum dots and nanoscale optical devices, leading to increased absorption and light emission rates. Furthermore, we have optimised various QD configurations to achieve high absorption rates of the resonant mode and prompt emission; the corresponding far-field radiation patterns are presented. By analysing these findings, insights can be gained into the spatial characteristics of the near and far field, enabling the development of novel light sources for optical communication and display technologies.

Nanomechanical measurements on silicate glass and on a polymer obtained ultrafast from a melt reveal distinct responses when differing thresholds of mechanical pressure are exceeded. Below a particular pressure, materials resist mechanical deformation similar to solids, but beyond this pressure, they exhibit deformation similar to liquids. This pressure, which varies with strain rate and is specific to each material, serves as a clear dividing line between two mechanisms of protection provided by "plastic" forces. One mechanism provides protection at lower pressures, acting through temporary mechanisms, while the other mechanism provides protection at higher pressures, acting through permanent rearrangements. This distinction allows for a understanding of how these two mechanisms contribute to the overall resilience of "amorphous" materials.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded of up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between decoration at the top and hollow sites. Furthermore, the system's induced magnetism is thoroughly examined.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our objective is to create a straightforward simulation of a supernova event replicating the shape, dimensions, and placement of Sgr A East, which was achieved using a simplified hydrodynamic model that simulated the development of a supernova remnant within the vicinity of the Galactic center. This area comprises a close-by large molecular cloud with which Sgr A East interacts, and the wind from the galactic center's dense star cluster. According to our most preferred remnant models, Sgr A East's age would be around 10 thousand years old. Additionally, suitable solutions were discovered for older ages but none existed for ages under 5 thousand years. Our simulations suggest the supernova event likely occurred 30 parsecs away from the galactic center, placed below the cloud's plane, expanding in a slightly inclined direction from the plane's surface, facing towards the east. Expanding into the wind from the galactic center's dense star cluster, the remnant exhibits an unusually high average velocity rate of about 10 to 20 km/s/m.

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. The outcomes suggest that using oversampling methods improves the accuracy of classification and highlights the superiority of using K-means and TF-IDF for document representation, with KNN showing comparable results to more complex neural networks. The study also indicates that KNN and SVM outperform other algorithms in dealing with class imbalance in text classification tasks.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset, we reproducted trends observed by Vendevin et al. in 2021, who found a correlation between national COVID deaths and local news coverage in top U.S. markets. Our research reveals similar results, but also reveals additional correlations. We discovered correlations between COVID coverage and local deaths in key markets, and correlations between regional hospitalizations and coverage in other markets. Our study shows that these results persist even when controlling for news outlet characteristics, such as ownership and audience demographics. Furthermore, we found that some demographic groups, like older and lower-income individuals, receive less COVID information from local news.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of cross-sectional ratios in electron proton collisions, drawing on JLab polarization experiments measuring the ratio of Sachs form factors in such interactions. Calculations considering a scenario with fully correlated kinematics reveal that variations in the electromagnetic properties of the proton could potentially be at odds with the achievable precision in experimental measurements. However, researchers can mitigate this risk by exploring free-boundary nuclear physics where the target proton's momentum transfers are both smaller and more evenly distributed across a broader $Q^2$ range than in individual nucleon-scattering experiments. For instance, using  ${}^{3}$He as a target at JLab could achieve precision of 6% or better, while targets like lithium or water at the EIC could achieve precision of 8% or better over an even broader range. Furthermore, our findings also demonstrate that the influence of the electromagnetic properties of the neutron is not significant in such measurements.

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach seeks to train an auxiliary policy that mimics a given target policy, and we introduce the concept of synthetic states to improve data efficiency. By generating synthetic states in conjunction with target reward signals, the learning rate of policy cloning can be significantly improved without compromising its theoretical and computational simplicity. Through rigorous reward functions and diverse dynamic systems, our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in accurately mimicking target policies, particularly in challenging environments characterized by complex dynamics and rare events.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been carried out utilizing the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The research explores both scenarios where Higgs bosons do not form resonances and those where they do, along with different Higgs branching ratios. It identifies that in the Standard Model framework, no production of $W/hh$ or $Z/hh$ boson pairs exceeding 87 inverse femtobarns, $W/hh$ boson pairs exceeding 72 inverse femtobarns, or $Z/hh$ boson pairs exceeding 62 inverse femtobarns at a 95 percent confidence level has been observed. Furthermore, the study provides boundaries at a 95 percent confidence level for how much the electroweak Standard Model is modified, influencing Higgs boson pair production.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and feedback systems 
are capable of offering highly sensitive detection at a broad spectrum range, 
which makes them suitable for detecting extremely weak magnetic fields or the 
faint signals from individual atoms. In order to improve the technology's ability 
to resolve frequency shifts, it's essential to accurately determine the frequency 
modulation spectrum. Traditionally, this is done by recollecting data after a 
processing step, which can't take advantage of the real-time and frequency resolution 
capabilities of the system. We've developed a new method that enables real-time 
frequency power spectrum estimation, allowing us to leverage the system's frequency 
resolution when operating at various levels of amplitude. This technique provides 
accurate results, can operate in a wide spectrum of frequencies, and is adaptable 
for applications involving large frequency ranges, such as detecting the faint 
signals from individual atoms.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem and from the characteristics of a derived K3 surface.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model with a $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ hidden sector gauge sector, where the hidden sector neutralino is lighter than its visible counterpart, leading to a loop-suppressed radiative decay process. The computation demonstrates that the visible sector neutralino can decay with a lifetime greater than the age of the universe. The detectability of this scenario lies in the indirect observation of a signature decay product into the hidden sector neutralino accompanied by a high-energy gamma ray photon, accessible through Fermi-LAT and future SKA, CTA experiments. Several benchmark cases align with existing astrophysical data and are consistent with the current experimental limits from collider searches and direct detection experiments, including the DAMA/LIBRA annual modulation signal.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface area enclosing box around a given set of points in three-dimensional space. Furthermore, building upon established hardness findings related to two-dimensional space, we adapt these results to a 3D setting characterized by specific types of graph structures derived from cutting planes procedures.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages often shrouded in mystery.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino background in future experiments measuring the scattering of neutrons, and even analyze the orientation of nuclei in solid targets. The possibility of reaching this goal in liquid detectors depends on various factors, including their micro-patterned gaseous detectors. This demonstration showcases a proof-of-concept for directly inferring the direction of nuclear recoils in a silicon target within a fibre-optically-read micro-patterned-segmented-gas-filled-chamber. The latter is characterized by numerous thin cathodes that preclude tracking the recoil trajectory, yet still manages to provide directional information. Its functionality is studied through simultaneous analysis of ionization topography patterns derived from light and charge signals. The experiment consists of a 2 cm^2 silicon wafer situated within a 1 mm-gap-filled micro-patterned-gas-filled-chamber containing 40 thin cathodes. Their spatial periodicity is such that each cathode measures 320 mm in length and 66.7 microns apart from their neighbours. The detector features 25 read-out photodetectors spread uniformly over its surface. This setup enables the reconstruction of ionization topography patterns, and consequently, the determination of recoil directions. The experimental setup employs a Pentane-based gas mixture with a high proportion of methane, operating at an electric field

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions, among others. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavioral data insights, often struggle to account for individual differences and contextual dependencies. To address these limitations, we've developed a multifaceted framework for evaluating commercial driving behavior, taking into account drivers' personal traits, operational habits, and environmental factors. By integrating contextual information and behavioral data, our approach enables more precise and fair driver assessments, ultimately informing road safety improvements. Applying our framework to a massive dataset of behavioral data can help identify patterns and trends in commercial driving behavior, providing data-driven insights for improved road safety practices.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and extracting text from rotated shapes.
The baseline models established for the competition leveraged a combination of state-of-the-art Advanced Pre-trained Appetizer (APA) features, trained with Novelty-Aware Loss (NAL), to overcome the challenge.
The base model for the holistic task achieved a high CER of 6.54% on unseen data.
The base model for the shape task exhibited a BER of 25.93% on unseen data.
During the competition, the model yielded a BER of 24.33@1% on the test set.
The model's performance was further enhanced by integrating the Direct Addresser (DAR) model.
The integrated model for the holistic task delivered a BER of 4.93@1% on the test set.
The integrated model for the shape task demonstrated a BER of 12.53@1% on the test set

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about the link between their dynamic behaviors and geometric properties of the underlying spaces they're defined within. To address this gap, a numerical method was proposed to classify random fields based on their spatial patterns by quantifying their local homogeneity using a metric that measures distance between random variable distributions. This approach showed that by analyzing the spatial patterns of random fields, scientists can better understand their influences on system dynamics and properties. This insight has the potential to help scientists understand and predict the transitions in system behaviors that arise when these patterns shift. To demonstrate the method's capabilities, it was applied to simple random processes and their characteristics were extracted, illustrating how the analysis could inform predictions about changes in system states. This framework's versatility extends beyond random fields to a broad range of statistical models, covering continuous and discrete spaces.

In our research, we conduct experiments examining the Rayleigh-Taylor Instability (RTI) in a two-dimensional framework. RTI occurs when lighter fluid is placed atop heavier fluid, causing density contrasts that lead to vortex formation. We studied the development of RTI by introducing a divider that separates the lighter from the heavier fluid initially, before the fluids are released and the instability unfolds. The divider's collapse generates a sequence of perturbations that resemble sinusoidal waves, with the sinusoidal shape transforming into an elliptical shape as perturbations travel downward and evolve into Taylor-Goldson Instability (TGI). The results demonstrate that TGI arises from three-dimensional disturbances triggered by the divider's instability. Moreover, we investigate the effects of various divider configurations on the development of RTI and observe that in some cases, the divider remains intact, preventing RTI from occurring.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$, and show that its algebraic component at critical point $m$ has bounded denominators when $G$ is a arithmetic symplectic group. As a result, the component can be expressed as an infinite product of terms involving Fourier-Jacobi expansions at point $\chi(q)^{-s}$ of automorphic cusp forms over $G$.

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions, researchers investigated how spin-dependent transport behaves in non-magnetic, graphene nanoribbons with different orientations of their transverse magnetic fields. Comparing normal and perpendicular orientations revealed a lack of spin polarization in the first, but its appearance in the second suggested new methods for creating spin-current sources in graphene nanoribbons could be explored further. Consistently, introducing an attractive interaction between electrons had a more significant effect on the spin polarization in perpendicular fields, leading to enhanced current generation.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion also includes a examination of the necessary conditions for the results obtained.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4 and a degree of at least (n-1)/2 for every vertex contains a pancyclic subgraph, which was later revealed by Erdos and Harary to be the best possible result. Later, a question was raised whether a graph on n vertices with a chromatic number of 3 and every pair of vertices having the same degree would necessarily contain a pancyclic subgraph. In this study, it is shown that such a graph on n vertices with n larger than 204, specifically a Moore-type graph, would necessarily contain a pancyclic subgraph. This answers an undocumented query proposed by Armbrust and Tyomkyn, who suggested that such a graph on n vertices with a chromatic number of 3 and every pair of vertices having the same degree would necessarily contain a pancyclic subgraph. In this study, a concrete value for n, which is 204, shows that a well-known three-distance graph, specifically a Moore-type graph, necessarily contains a pancyclic subgraph. A number of unresolved questions and conjectures are also brought up in this paper.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, zirconium-zirconium, and lead-lead collisions at a specific energy of 200 GeV has been studied in this research. This study utilized the CLVisc model to examine the development of uneven energy density, radial movement, and viscosity in these collisions. It was found that the uneven energy density distribution begins to take shape shortly after the initial collision, and this unevenness drives the movement of light particles. The research also found a connection between the radial movement of these collisions and the unevenness of the initial energy distribution, and it discovered that the initial unevenness of the energy distribution in square-shaped collisions is greater than that found in rounder collisions. Further, it was found that the unevenness of the energy distribution in these collisions is directly related to the variation in the movement of individual quarks, and this variation contributes to the formation of specific areas of high and low pressure in the collision. The study suggests that the initial unevenness of the energy distribution in these collisions could be used to identify and analyze specific areas of high pressure in these collisions, and this could potentially be a key factor in understanding and identifying the characteristics of matter with high density in these collisions.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to efficiently handle complex systems' state responses over time by locally approximating a system's behavior with a low-dimensional spectral basis. Despite its optimality in two-dimensional state spaces, ASK faces increasing computation demands with higher dimensional states. To mitigate these drawbacks, we developed the sparse-grid-based ASK (SG-ASK) method, which approximates the system's state space within a specified tolerance using a low-dimensional spectral basis on selectively sampled state space points. By leveraging properties of spectral methods, we incorporated an optimization step to determine the most relevant state space points for the basis at each time step. Numerical simulations demonstrate that SG-ASK can efficiently handle high-dimensional systems for long time horizons, achieving significant computation speedups of up to five orders of magnitude compared to traditional integration methods and other low-dimensional models such as Koopman and dynamic mode decomposition methods.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical difficulties in explaining ionization within the framework of quantum mechanics. The fundamental principles of resonance theory are then explored, and the exterior complex scaling method for extracting resonance parameters through the Schrodinger equation is comprehensively outlined. This approach is explained in the context of numerical solution via a finite element method for the scaled variable, and evidence from results for a one-dimensional hydrogen atom in an Coulomb field supports the effectiveness of this technique. The theory is then developed further for a two-body system in a Coulomb field in three-dimensional space, with a specific exploration of the physically restricted domain within the scaled variable framework. This investigation leads to a derivation of Schrodinger's equation in the restricted domain for the scaled Hamiltonian via a Taylor series expansion, and subsequent infinitesimal change in the restricted domain is found to yield infinitesimal changes in the resonance parameters in the restricted domain within the scaled variable framework. The theoretical findings suggest that the restricted domain in the scaled variable framework has a flexible nature.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used method for solving the Schrödinger problem in terms of its efficiency. Nevertheless, the linear programming formulation fails in "degenerate situations," resulting in a variety of issues. Asperoukov was able to overcome these challenges by reformulating the problem using an auxiliary linear programming with a constrained negative semidefinite coefficient matrix. Building upon this concept, the presented paper introduces two new generalizations of the reformulation, followed by a proof of their mathematical validity. These new models offer alternative approaches to resolving degenerate cases, with one form offering a more efficient solution and a faster convergence rate.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states and yields a combined result. The calculated t¯t cross-section has a total uncertainty of 3.9% and amounts to 67.5 pb, which corresponds to 0.9 pb (statistical) ± 2.3 pb (systematic) ± 1.1 pb (lumi) ± 0.2 pb (syst, TT) pb-1. This outcome is consistent with theoretical quantum chromodynamic predictions and offers constraints on the proton's parton distribution functions at high energy.

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system or environment would influence the behavior of its core element. Researchers have recently investigated the impact of this concept in the context of systems that exhibit many-body localization, a state where random fluctuations prevent thermal behavior regardless of the driving energy levels. Core degrees of freedom typically display either simple oscillations or complex, often chaotic behavior. Interestingly, some core degrees of freedom show signs of both localized and delocalized states, a phenomenon known as bi-localization. These core degrees of freedom also exhibit other distinct properties, such as long-lasting fluctuations and atypical levels of excitations. All these traits can be fully understood if the core degrees of freedom are seen as navigating an "optimal path" in the system's many-body landscape, a concept known as Floquet Hamiltonian.
.
.
A key aspect of this "optimal path" is that it may display characteristics not seen at the individual component or system level. For example, it's possible for the core degrees of freedom to display localization even though the surrounding system does not, a phenomenon known as environmental protection of localization. Additionally, it's possible for the core degrees of freedom to display localization even though the core itself is not in a localized state, a phenomenon known as self-localization. All these traits can be seen in experiments involving 1D quantum drivers, where it's possible to see the core degrees of localization even though the surrounding system does not, a phenomenon known as non-equilibrium

${u}_{\alpha}(z)$ and ${u}_{\beta}(z)$ satisfy the subordination relationship 
$0 \le A + BzT_{A}(z) \le 1$, where $T_{A}(z)$ denotes the Tschakalowski 
transform of $A(z)$. This identifies specific sufficient conditions for $A$ and 
$B$ that uniquely maximize or minimize the real part of $z$ in the given 
subordination relationship. Several examples are also presented to illustrate 
the conditions discovered in this study.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million users in the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo, who exponentially increased their use of online dating platforms over a period of seven months in 2020, directly following strict lockdown measures. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a significant spike in users listing "no relationship" as their intention on these platforms, peaking at 42% and exceeding pre-lockdown levels by 9%. By applying a machine learning approach to user profile data, we identified clear patterns in users' behavioral changes. In contrast to prior research, our results indicate that users' increased online presence does not seem to be influenced by changes in income or job security, but rather by the prolonged period of being isolated from others in the urban environment of Sao Paulo.

This research focuses on an approach for managing computational complexity in the simulation of two-phase flow and transport. The approach involves a two-stage, field-separated nonlinear preprocessing technique for the coupled mass conservation equations. This preprocessing, composed of an oil wet and water wet relative permeability nonlinear field and an accumulation transport nonlinear field, ensures efficient computational management by dividing the Jacobian matrix into individual components for rapid convergence. The preprocessed system retains the same solutions as the combined system but significantly reduces computational time by allowing individual component optimization. This advanced preprocessing technique is capable of being integrated with existing numerical methods and can be implemented in complex simulations of oil-water flows accompanied by accumulation transport. The efficiency of this preprocessing has been successfully tested in simulations of oil-water flows accompanied by accumulation transport in a rough porous medium. The results show the preprocessed approach produces accurate results in a reduced number of operations compared to the conventional algorithm.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life forms to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specificity in relation to its own orientation, making the interaction between chiral matter and light a highly effective means of distinguishing between the various forms of chirality. When light signals interact with the matter, they may be discriminated based on certain characteristics using a novel chiral system linked to light, consisting of artificial units able to process chirality efficiently and enhance signaling efficiency. We utilize the fact that certain metals, such as platinum, exhibit a natural linkage capable of transferring the chirality of organic molecules effectively, thus enabling a more precise and efficient method of communicating chirality between organic and metal surfaces. Our research demonstrates, using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, that enantiomers of chiral adenosine monophosphate (AMP) are distinguishable when interacting with a surface covered in a layer of platinum and treated with a vaporized chiral molecule. This development represents significant advancements in the artificial recognition and discrimination of chirality based on light signals, as well as the use of chiral metal surfaces, including platinum, through contactless interaction methods, though the itself surface is not capable of distinguishing right from left direction, thus it does not exhibit chirality, yet it shows a particular way of interacting with it.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model. This match, however, is confined to the boundary of the unit disk in the Liouville CFT. We also explore the Witten diagrams of the time-like CFT, establishing connections with the random matrix theories proposed by Douglas and Vaula. Furthermore, we evaluate the semi-classical wave function of the JT gravity using the Schwinger-Dyson mechanism and show that it displays characteristics of two-dimensional conformal field theory completeness.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This research extends our previous solutions by applying the Einstein equations to the warp drive metric, incorporating both a perfect fluid source and a perfect fluid source with a cosmological constant, including a special case with a perfect fluid source and no cosmological constant, previously found by the researchers ( arXiv:2101.11467 ). These new solutions have led to the connection between warp drive, shock waves, and Burgers equations, via the Hopf-Cauchy problem for the one-dimensional Burgers equation. However, it appears challenging to achieve the reverse transformation, from Einstein equations to the Burgers equation, likely due to additional geometric constraints. Moreover, imposing the geometric conditions on the shift vector further narrows down the allowed perfect fluid sources for the warp drive metric. Finally, the researchers have revealed that the shift vector, rather than the spatial vector, is responsible for achieving an acceptable perfect fluid source, thus shedding light on the role of the shift vector in warp drive theory.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, assessing risks, and estimating costs. Determining the condition and interconnections of their underground systems presents a significant hurdle for cities. An effective maintenance approach involves an accurate estimation of asset life expectancy based on the current condition of the infrastructure. A recent study developed an initial model for estimating the life expectancy of underground infrastructure assets based on the current condition of the roads. However, this model has several limitations, enabling this research to explore alternative data and methods to improve life expectancy predictions. A machine learning algorithm, the Long-Short-Term-Memory-Net, was applied to the set of road condition time series data collected for each asset type. The results indicate that the LSTM-Net model performed better than the initial model in predicting the life expectancy of utilities when provided with sufficient data. Conversely, the results showed that the initial model still performs competitively in cases where the utility company's time series data is limited. Therefore, recommending that utilities and municipalities rely on a combination of traditional engineering methods and machine learning techniques to gain a more comprehensive understanding of their infrastructure assets.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized the interaction between optical dipoles. By computing the second-order optical response of the object, we accounted for the effects of both the quasi-molecular dipole series and individual dipoles. This approach allowed us to quantify the impact of spin dephasing on the two-dimensional structure. Notably, our research indicates that, at a temperature of 30 mK, the primary contributors to spin dephasing comprise the quasi-molecular dipole transitions and ion motion. The resulting dephasing time is approximately 3 seconds. Moreover, we discovered that, under these conditions, the primary limitations on the resolution are associated with the object's depth and optical focus diameter rather than the wavelength of the light used. Specifically, a focus diameter of 2 micrometers and a 3D depth of approximately 5 micrometers are found to be the main constraints on resolution, allowing for a maximum achievable resolution of approximately 6 nanometers. This result suggests the possibility of achieving nanometer-scale resolution.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. A significant factor in producing TERS signals is the electromagnetic field produced by the plasmonic tips utilized in this procedure. The electromagnetic field generated by these plasmonic tips has two primary influences: the localized field near its apex and the field at a short distance away from it. Our research experimentally examines the electromagnetic field created by a sharp silver tip at a short distance, and it also collects TERS spectra using the same tip. By modeling these fields, we discovered that they have distinct orientations, which significantly affects the combination of the field's polarization and orientation at the sample surface. Consequently, this principle has the potential to greatly enhance TERS precision. To achieve this, we introduced a novel approach, involving the utilization of two tips with perpendicular polarization, to greatly enhance resolution. Our simulations also imply that a critical tip characteristic, the "kink angle," plays a vital role in optimizing the field's quality and resolution. Our research provides substantial evidence to understand the characteristics of these fields and to devise novel methods to greatly enhance the precision of TERS.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope (SRT) to observe the sources surrounding PSR J1559+0529, a pulsar located near the center of the UU Gemini radio filaments complex. Our 10 GHz radio observations with a high angular resolution (3.5 arcseconds) detected the pulsar as its primary emission source, with no significant radiation or diffuse emission detected around it. These results set an upper limit on the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning tori around the pulsar, especially compared to previous 20 GHz measurements from the Cerra Somma Radio Telescope (CSRT). Our 10 GHz measurements produced an AME upper limit nearly two times that of the CSRT, indicating that the UU Gemini radio filaments do not likely originate from spin tori surrounding the pulsar.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and additional neutron scattering experiments. In contrast to the previously assumed, albeit widely adopted model of entropy involving disorder across the high-symmetry phase's mirror plane, it is now clear that this simplistic model is invalid. Instead, it is discovered that the significant entropy originates from the low-frequency wobbling of ammonium ions in this phase, which produces small to negligible harmonic components. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for vibrational entropy stemming from broad energy minima, which may be just as significant as configurational entropy due to crystallographic disorder in discovering molecular materials with functional properties.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, which is distinct from the optimal strategy, maximization, that consistently selects the most rewarding option, even when the options' reward probabilities vary over time.  Maximization is equivalent to a heuristic called maximax, which focuses on the highest possible outcome, which is different from another heuristic, maximin, that focuses on the highest guaranteed outcome. Previous studies have found that humans, particularly children, employ an assortment-learning strategy, which is characterized by an increase in the probability of choosing an assortment with a higher maximum payoff over time. Now, an experimental study in Nature Scientific Reports, titled "Maximixation: A learning strategy for dealing with uncertain rewards", suggests that a theoretical version of the strategy, called maximixation, is able to effectively account for probability distributions, which are often unknown, thereby distinguishing it from the related maximax and maximin strategies. Additionally, the study also found that maximixation is capable of explaining a recent discovery that children, particularly those as young as 3 years old, are more likely to choose an assortment with a higher potential reward at lower probability levels, which is less common than choosing an assortment with a higher potential reward at higher probability levels.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 planes, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 monopoles using a complex that operates under the symmetry of E8. We've established that E8 roots correspond to directions within a 4D complex space consisting of a 3D complex space and a plane. Each E8 root has a counterpart that specifies a direction in this plane. We've also found a relationship similar to the one seen in the Witting configuration, where vectors corresponding to the same unitary irreducible representation of the U(3) group, with spin-3/2 as a U(3) subgroup of SU(8), point in the same direction in this complex space. We've observed that the weights of this representation, acting as vectors in U(3) space, can be found through a configuration where they are evenly spaced on a circle. We've also seen that the group SU(8)-U(3) plays a key role in this configuration by pointing to a relationship between spin-3/2 monopole solutions of the Einstein equation and irreducible representations of this group. Further study of these monopole solutions, where the Witting configuration provides a new perspective, could lead to insights into their properties.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing a series of improvements for Lp space. The results include a new result showing that a specific data structure can solve the problem in log(n) time with an improved complexity in L1 space, while building upon previous work in L2 space. Additionally, it offers competitive upper bounds in L2 space and tight lower bounds in L1 and L4 spaces. Further, it extends the findings to more complex objects like point sets, surface meshes, and cumulative distribution functions, introducing a linear-sized data structure that allows for efficient nearest neighbor searches in these object spaces with an approximation factor, particularly in C- spaces. The results have applications in areas like metric search, curve comparison, and similarity search.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively.

When humans operate robots in complex tasks and navigate through uncertain environments, they often infer the robot's intentions based on past interactions and make educated guesses about its behavior. However, robots currently have no way to know what humans think they can reasonably expect from each other. As a result, robots cannot convey their own strategies or strategies that humans could use, limiting the potential for more effective collaboration. In order to improve assistive teleoperation and increase productivity, robots should be able to detect what humans think they can reasonably expect from each other. In our study, a robot uses the observations of a trained sensor to infer what a human thinks it can reasonably expect from each other during tasks that require assistance. In our experiments, both the human and the robot performed together in a slinging process and we used a machine learning approach to teach the robot how to detect the human's strategy. In our results, the robot was able to successfully identify the human's strategy in 65% of the observations, demonstrating potential for further improvement in both the observations and the results. In addition, a study was conducted to see if the results would improve if the human's strategy was clearer and if more observations were taken, and indeed the results showed that the results improved significantly. In order to show the potential of this approach, a study was conducted to see if the results could be used in real-time and indeed the results showed that the results could be used in real-time. In conclusion, a robot approach was proposed to detect what

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, using multiple sensors to gather comprehensive three-dimensional information is essential. While, in practice, using a single RGB-D sensor provides a reasonable initial approach, employing a 3D LiDAR scanner allows for a more efficient and precise environment mapping and object detection process. Nevertheless, integrating LiDAR data with other sensor types, like cameras, poses significant challenges. An advanced new system has been developed to integrate LiDAR data and RGB-D information for constructing and maintaining detailed 3D maps, particularly for large unfamiliar environments. This new system utilizes a dedicated 3D point cloud pruning technique, which significantly reduces processing time, allowing it to generate highly accurate 3D maps and object pruning parameters in near real-time. Additionally, a novel LiDAR-based object detector has been created to identify various large and small distinct objects, even when they are partially or fully occluded. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this new system in generating accurate 3D maps and object detection methods, surpassing current best practices in the field.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with negative values is gaining momentum in study as their positive counterparts exhibit exceptional performance in various wireless communication applications. To facilitate efficient algorithm development for array analysis, we propose introducing a novel graph-based model, incorporating traditional array concepts. This model offers a concise representation of array-related problems, enabling swift detection of key characteristics and interdependencies. Our framework has widespread applicability to diverse array-related issues, and we highlight its utility in addressing critical problems related to array pattern design. By leveraging our graph model, researchers and developers can access an integrated platform for solving array-related problems, supporting model creation, parameter calculation, and optimization. We anticipate this framework to serve as a foundation for future algorithm development, enhancing our understanding of unique array properties and facilitating model reductions, feature extractions, and other transformations.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Customized algorithms are usually developed specifically for these sources, which may cause reconstructed images to contain calibration errors. In an effort to eliminate these errors, we introduce an advanced algorithm that can determine the source energy spectrum directly from CT data, without the need for prior information on the spectrum. Additionally, by using an example, we demonstrate the efficacy of this spectrum correction method in producing reconstructed CT images that are both denser and less noisy.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this with a control scenario where these effects are absent. We apply a theoretical framework that combines both quantum and classical principles, leading to a simplified representation of the metal's behavior through a quantum-inspired local response model and a classical nonlocal response model. It's observed that the local response model diverges for certain parameter conditions due to unphysical field enhancements. Conversely, the nonlocal response model doesn't exhibit such divergences and accurately predicts attenuation or amplification of the incident light, depending on its frequency, distance between the metallic regions, and electron scattering frequency in the gap. We experimentally verify the nonlocal model by examining the attenuation of the incident light and the spillover effect on the fluorescence signal from atomic layers near the metallic edge.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that enhanced results can be achieved when users also specify the relative significance of those terms. Although CNER bears some resemblance to related concepts such as List Question answering and Entity disambiguation, its primary goal is to gather user feedback to dynamically construct a class of entity profiles and leverage this data for extracting entities from unrestricted text. Our focus in CNER involves identifying relevant sentences containing entities similar to a selected query entity. Our findings show that having users help in selecting context-bearing terms and weight them yields better performance over CNER systems that rely solely on automated methods. Furthermore, we found that using human-provided weights leads to improved larsson CNER performance as well as better generalization when compared to systems that rely on automated methods.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, involving discrete or continuous values, errors, cumulative totals, or event recordings. Expected features of multivariate time series include non-stationarity, non-linearity, non-normality, correlations, shocks, trends, seasonalities, changes in trends, comovement, interdependence, and unexpected events. Modern advanced time series techniques aim to detect, prevent, forecast, assess, and mitigate the impact of discrete and continuous events. Real-world multivariate time series data often comprises individual, anomalous, normal, critical, and irrelevant events, deserving careful analysis. Acquired multivariate time series data may encompass sensor readings, financial transactions, human behavior, system logs, physical law governances, astronomical observations, etc., serving as a window into the happenings of the world, its living entities, and the interactions within, between, and among them. Multivariate time series analysis techniques are rapidly evolving, with recent research employing methods from artificial intelligence, probabilistic models, regression models, latent factor representations, visualizations, rankings, embeddings, and related data abstraction strategies. As global interconnectedness grows, the management, preservation, and evaluation of high-dimensional time-based data have become essential, involving complex decisions on data sourcing, data processing, data analysis, and data presentation. Multivariate time series data exploration and visualization, data representation, and reasoning methods are essential in facilitating access to, understanding of, and impact of such data. The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in decision-making to enhance overall healthcare quality. Advances in recent years have seen the development of EHR standards and EHR-related data sets, leading to breakthroughs in text and knowledge processing applied to EHRs. Despite initial challenges with EHR data, today's sophisticated EHR systems offer comprehensive and detailed patient information. As healthcare systems continue to evolve, EHRs will play a pivotal role in decision-making processes. In this context, this paper aims to provide a thorough examination of EHRs, covering key topics, including EHR standards, EHR data sets, and advanced machine learning applications in EHRs.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions within the boundary using coupled differential equations, including the Poisson equation. We discover that solvent effects profoundly impact the electrostatic potential, ion counts, and dimension of the boundary layer, especially in low salt concentrations and near charged flexible surfaces. Furthermore, our study reveals that solvent effects on the electrostatic potential and ion counts become more pronounced as the degree of flexible charging increases and the ionic strength decreases. These findings also apply to sodium caseinate, an example of a charged flexible material.

Automating the labor-intensive and one-by-one identification of requirements in unstructured text is a highly desirable goal for many organizations. To this end, NLP has become a crucial component in the requirements engineering field, enabling the design of systems to uncover implicit patterns within unorganized text. Our solution, a multi-stage engine, comprises a network architecture that leverages Chebychev polynomials for producing a detailed map of the requirements discovery process. Our approach has been successfully tested using 260 unique sentences extracted from existing datasets, yielding a notable 85% accuracy in manually reviewing and verifying the requirements extraction outcome.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique.
